struct a binary search tree T containing the items in A such that T has height O(log n). You
may assume n is one less than a power of two.
Solution: Assume n = 2k −1. We begin by sorting the array A using merge sort. Then,
we build our binary tree as follows: If our current array has length 1, insert it into the tree.
Otherwise, insert the middle element into the tree and recurse on the two halves of the array,
which have length 2k−1 −1, keeping a pointer to our current ”root” so that we can insert the
next elements easily. By induction on k, the height of the resulting tree is k −1 ∈O(log n).

Problem 1.
A frog is attempting to cross a river by jumping on stones. The river is divided into units of length,
and at each unit, there may or may not be a stone. The frog can jump on a stone, but not on water.
The frog begins on the first stone and must reach the last stone. If the frog’s last jump had length
k, then the next jump must be of length k −1, k, or k + 1 units (but all jumps must be positive).
The frog may only move in the forward direction and begins by making a jump of length 1 unit.
Given an array stones of integers in strictly increasing order, representing the positions of the
stones in the river, determine whether the frog can reach the final stone.
Example 1. Input: stones = [0,1,3,5,6,8,11,15]
Output: true
Explanation: The frog can jump from position 0 →1 →3 →5 →6 →8

Review: Binary Search
• Input: (static) array A of n numbers in non-decreasing order, and a target number t.
• Output: number of indices i such that A[i] < t.
• Example: [2, 3, 4, 8, 9], 5 7→3
• Brute force algorithm (iterating over the entire array) takes Θ(n) time, but we can do better
with divide and conquer!
• Divide and conquer algorithm: recursively divide the array in half, and search only one half.
– Base case: if A is empty, output 0.
– Recursive step: compare t and A[m], where m := ⌊n/2⌋.
* If t ≤A[m], search prefix A[: m] for t and output the result.
* If A[m] < t, search suffix A[m + 1 :] for t, add m + 1, and output the sum.

• If we ever find a poly-time algorithm for any NP-complete problem, it would yield a poly-
time algorithm for all problems in NP.
• Contrapositive: if P̸ = NP, then any NP-complete problem cannot have a poly-time algo-
rithm.
• The punchline: many different NP-complete problems known including subset sum, longest
simple path, 3-colorability, and 3SAT! In decades, no efficient algorithm found for any of
them. Therefore, all are very likely to not have efficient algorithms.
• What if P = NP? A world where brute-force search is unnecessary and creativity can be
automated!
– Could find proof of any true mathematical statement (which has a polynomial-size
proof) in polynomial time – no more need for 6.1210 lecturers!
– Public-key cryptography would be impossible!

Lecture 23: Complexity
• In complexity-class language, NP ⊆EXPTIME.
• In fact, can show P ⊆NP ⊆PSPACE ⊆EXPTIME.
• The million dollar question (literally!): is P = NP? We don’t know, but strongly believe
that P̸ = NP!
Some more NP problems
• Example 1: 3-colorability.
– Input x: an undirected graph G
– Desired output: YES if every vertex in G can be assigned one of three colors, such that
no edge connects two vertices of the same color.
– Certificate c: a coloring of the graph.
– Verifier: Loop through edges and check that the given certificate c assigns the endpoints
distinct colors.
• Example 2: 3SAT
– Input x: a formula in Boolean variables of a special form: an “and” of “clauses,” each

Lecture 17: Greedy Algorithms
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Brynmor Chapman, Srini Devadas, Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Will Leiserson
Lecture 17: Greedy Algorithms
Greedy Choice Property
• Shortest Paths algorithms used the Optimal Sub-Problem Property: An optimal solution to a
problem contains optimal solutions to its sub-problems.
• With Greedy Algorithms, we can make the decision to solve the problem locally, without the
need to solve the sub-problems first. So a Greedy Algorithm is an iterative algorithm that
makes locally optimal choices one by one.
• Greedy Algorithms rely on the Greedy Choice Property, which dictates that a locally optimal
decision (the “greedy choice”) can always be extended into a globally optimal solution.
• The Greedy Choice

Lecture 10: Graph Search
Correctness
• Claim: DFS visits v and correctly sets P(v) for every vertex v reachable from s
• Proof: induct on k, for claim on only vertices within distance k from s
– Base case (k = 0): P(s) is set correctly for s and s is visited
– Inductive step: Consider vertex v with δ(s, v) = k′ + 1
– Consider vertex u, the second to last vertex on some shortest path from s to v
– By induction, since δ(s, u) = k′, DFS visits u and sets P(u) correctly
– While visiting u, DFS considers v ∈Adj(u)
– Either v is in P, so has already been visited, or v will be visited while visiting u
– In either case, v will be visited by DFS and will be added correctly to P
Running Time
• Algorithm visits each vertex u at most once and spends O(1) time for each v ∈Adj(u)
• Work upper bounded

one-way sea routes between them. Every time one of Jack’s ships enters a port p, it must pay a tax of t(p)

Is Our Subset Sum Algorithm Polynomial Time?
• Input size is n + 1: one integer L and n integers in A
• Is O(nL) bounded above by a polynomial in n + 1? NO, not necessarily
• On w-bit word RAM, L ≤2w and w ≥lg(n + 1), but we don’t have an upper bound on w

Pseudopolynomial
• Algorithm runs in pseudopolynomial time: running time is bounded above by a constant-
degree polynomial in input size and input integers
• Such algorithms are polynomial in the case that integers are polynomially bounded in input
size, i.e., nO(1) (same case that Radix Sort runs in O(n) time)
• Counting sort O(n + u), radix sort O(n logn u), direct-access array build O(n + u)

Problem 3.
Diagonalization
(a) Give a concrete, computable function f such that for every polynomial time algorithm
B, for cofinitely many inputs x, B(x) halts in at most (not asymptotically) f(|x|) time.
Solution: Many functions will work, e.g. f(n) = 2n.
(b) Construct (with proof) a decider A such that for every polynomial time algorithm B,
for infinitely many inputs x, we have A(x)̸ = B(x). You may assume a computable
bijection ϕ that maps strings to pairs of strings.
Solution: Define A as follows:
Input is x
Let (B, y) = ϕ(x)
Run B for f(|x|) steps on input x
Return the opposite result (or if B(x) hasn’t terminated yet, output YES)
This algorithm always halts (in exponential time with f(n) = 2n), so is a decider.

relationships.snippet: In the comparison model, how much time is required...?
In the comparison model, binary search is the optimal find in a sorted array
In the comparison model, binary search is the optimal find in a sorted array

Because the input strings are binary, differentiating between them puts us in the comparison model (is A[i] positive or negative?). To be able to produce any of n −1 different outputs, we require at least Ω(log n) input reads, i.e. Ω(log n) worst-case runtime.
By restricting to binary inputs, we remove all super-constant branching from decision trees, so every algorithm becomes a comparison algorithm.

Lecture 16: All Pairs Shortest Paths
Why study all-pairs shortest paths?
Reason 1: It is useful in its own right.
• If you run a large network (communication, transport, etc.) you might want to compute all
shortest paths at once up front so that you can quickly answer shortest-path queries later on.
Reason 2: Fast algorithms for APSP give fast algorithms for many other problems.
• Virginia Vassilevska Williams and Ryan Williams showed (2010) that APSP is equivalent, in
a certain formal sense, to a number of other problems:
– Finding negative triangles in a graph
– Finding the minimum-weight cycle in a graph (with non-negative edge weights)
– The replacement-paths problem (find a path from here to there avoiding all edges on the
shortest path).
– . . .

Name:

(c) [15 points] Moving along an edge (u, v) costs Wooper s(u, v) mL of slime, where s(u, v) is a positive
rational number. Eating a Rare Candy allows Wooper to produce 1mL more slime each time he moves
along an edge in the future. Give an algorithm to determine whether or not Wooper can wander forever
without running out of slime. For full credit, your algorithm should be as efficient as possible. Analyze
runtime, but you need not prove correctness. You may assume that Wooper can start with an arbitrary
finite amount of slime. You may also assume a working solution to part (b), even if you did not solve it
yourself.
Solution:
Weight each edge (u, v) in G by s(u, v) −r(u). Wooper can wander forever iff a non-
positive cycle exists. Run Bellman-Ford from s in G.

(d) [3 points] If A ≤p B and there is an algorithm for A that runs in polynomial time, then there is an
algorithm for B that runs in polynomial time.
□TRUE
■FALSE
Solution:
We can only infer that if B is solvable in polynomial time, then A is too, but not the converse. B could
be a way harder problem than A. For example, let B be an extremely hard decision problem of which
we know an easy YES-input y and an easy NO-input x. Then A could just be any polynomial-time
solvable decision problem (say s-t REACHABILITY), and the ‘transformation’ of inputs (that shows
A ≤p B) is one that takes inputs in A, solves A by itself, and outputs y if the answer is supposed to be
yes, or x otherwise.

1. In an undirected graph, a clique is a set of vertices such that every pair of them is connected
by an edge. Given an undirected graph G = (V, E) and an integer k, CLIQUE asks whether
G has a clique of size k.
Show that CLIQUE is in NP by designing a verifier for it: specify what the certificates
represent, describe the verifier itself, analyze its runtime, and argue that the verifier takes
polynomial time in n, the size of the input.
Solution: A certificate is a set of nodes U which is a clique of size k.
The verifier first checks that |U| = k. Then it checks that for all u, v ∈U, there is an edge
(u, v) ∈E.
This takes O(k2) time. Since k ≤|V | ≤n (because the input includes G which has size
|V | + |E|), this is O(n2).
It turns out that CLIQUE is NP-complete!

one-way sea routes between them. Every time one of Jack’s ships enters a port p, it must pay a tax of t(p)

• Before we leave the subject of graph algorithms, we should see least one algorithm that
exploits the fact that we can view graphs as matrices.
• The juice we get from treating graphs as matrices is that there are fast algorithms for multiplying
matrices.

– Naïve algorithm: 𝑂(𝑛3) time.

– The basic trick is reminiscent of the Karatsuba trick we saw at the start of the course for
fast multiplication of integers.

matrix-multiplication algorithms.

integer is in the range [0, n2). What is the runtime of the fastest algorithm to sort A lexicographically?
Select the one best answer.
□Θ(n)

□Θ(n log n)
□Θ(n2)
Solution: Tuple sort with radix sort as auxiliary. Since radix sort isn’t in place and input size is ω(n),
it is important to use a length n array of pointers instead of copying and modifying the original array.
Each of the log log n radix sorts then takes O(n) time, and the input array can be overwritten once at
the end. This is optimal because it takes Ω(n log log n) time to read the input.

4. Describe how to implement DFS using a STACK as the main data structure. Remember that
a STACK supports the push and pop operations.
Solution:
Initialize the Stack to contain just the source vertex. Repeat while the stack is
nonempty:
• pop the first element off the stack.
– If it is marked, move to the next round
– If it is not marked, mark it as visited. Besides, for each of its neighbors, push the
neighbor to the stack.
.
The time complexity of this implementation is also O(|E|) because we process each vertex
and each edge at most once, and (for single-source) discover at most |E| + 1 vertices. We
could do the same for a full (rather than single-source) DFS, which would still take time
O(|V | + |E|).

6.1210 Midterm 2 Review
Name:
4 of 8
(h) [3 points] If G is a binary tree, then the finishing order of DFS (starting from the root and processing
children from left to right) is always the same as:
□The PRE-ORDER traversal
□The IN-ORDER traversal
■The POST-ORDER traversal
□Neither
Solution:
A DFS will finish its out-going edges first, then finish the current node. As there are no cycles, the left
sub-tree will finish before the right sub-tree is visited. After the right sub-tree is finished, the root is
finished.

6.1210 Midterm 2 Review
Name:
4 of 8
(h) [3 points] If G is a binary tree, then the finishing order of DFS (starting from the root and processing
children from left to right) is always the same as:
□The PRE-ORDER traversal
□The IN-ORDER traversal
■The POST-ORDER traversal
□Neither
Solution:
A DFS will finish its out-going edges first, then finish the current node. As there are no cycles, the left
sub-tree will finish before the right sub-tree is visited. After the right sub-tree is finished, the root is
finished.

you should refer to “strongly connected components” if you are talking about the notion

The condensation graph
To understand the structure of a directed graph, it can be useful to look at the graph of its strongly
connected components. We call this the condensation graph.
More formally, given a directed graph G, the condensation graph Gcon is a directed graph that
we define as follows:
• The vertices of Gcon correspond to strongly connected components of G. We will label these
C1, . . . , Ck.
• There is an edge (Ci, Cj) in Gcon iff there exists an edge (u, v) in G with u ∈Ci and v ∈Cj.

Proof. The graph Gcon is directed by definition. We need to show that it is acyclic. We will do this
by contradiction. Suppose that Gcon has a cycle Ci1 →Ci2 →· · · →Cim →Ci1, with m > 1.
Then we claim that all vertices in Ci1 and Ci2 are in the same SCC, which is impossible since these
SCCs were distinct by assumption. Indeed, there is a path from any vertex in Ci1 to any vertex in
Ci2 by going around the cycle forwards, and there is a path from any vertex in Ci2 to any vertex in
Ci1 by going all the way around the cycle from Ci2 to Ci3, Ci4, and so on until we return to Ci1.

Pseudopolynomial

degree polynomial in input size and input integers
• Such algorithms are polynomial in the case that integers are polynomially bounded in input
size, i.e., nO(1) (same case that Radix Sort runs in O(n) time)
• Counting sort O(n + u), radix sort O(n logn u), direct-access array build O(n + u)

Meowth has n weighted coins numbered 0 through n −1. For every 0 ≤i < n, Meowth knows pi, the

Problem 1.
A frog is attempting to cross a river by jumping on stones. The river is divided into units of length,
and at each unit, there may or may not be a stone. The frog can jump on a stone, but not on water.
The frog begins on the first stone and must reach the last stone. If the frog’s last jump had length
k, then the next jump must be of length k −1, k, or k + 1 units (but all jumps must be positive).
The frog may only move in the forward direction and begins by making a jump of length 1 unit.
Given an array stones of integers in strictly increasing order, representing the positions of the
stones in the river, determine whether the frog can reach the final stone.
Example 1. Input: stones = [0,1,3,5,6,8,11,15]
Output: true
Explanation: The frog can jump from position 0 →1 →3 →5 →6 →8

11400da0-142d-479d-a2ab-7856bcffd1c7.definition: An operation on two functions f and g to produce a new function where (f ⋆ g)(x) = g(f(x)).

citations.snippet:
6.1210 Practice Final 2
Name:
12 of 12
• ∞is the zero function
• f ⋆g := g ◦f
• f ⪯g iff f(x) ≥g(x)
Monotonicity: suppose f ⪯g. Then f(x) ≥g(x). For any monotone function h, h(f(x)) ≥h(g(x)),
so f ⋆h ⪯g ⋆h.
Non-negativity: the identity function is the identity with respect to function composition. Both possible
edge weights are pointwise bounded above by the identity function.
Supremum: for every f : N →N, f(k) ≥0, i.e. f ⪯∞.
The weight w(π) of a path π maps k to the number of elephants remaining at the end of π if k elephants
start along π.
Run Dijkstra from (0, 0) and output δ((n −1, 0))(x) ≥100.
Note that the only way a weight w is ever used is to evaluate w(x). Therefore, when running Dijkstra,
we can represent a weight w by the single value w(x). Runtime is then O(n log n + |M| + |R|)

Run Dijkstra from (0, 0) and output δ((n −1, 0))(x) ≥100.

we can represent a weight w by the single value w(x). Runtime is then O(n log n + |M| + |R|)

Exercise: Acceptance Problem
The following problem, similar to the Halting Problem, is called the Acceptance Problem.
ACCEPT
Input: a binary string, interpreted as a pair (A, x)
– A is an algorithm
– x is some other binary string
Output:
– YES if A(x) eventually halts and outputs YES
– NO otherwise, i.e. if A(x) outputs NO or doesn’t halt
(a) Prove that ACCEPT is recognizable. That is, prove that there exists an algorithm B
such that B(A, x) = YES iff ACCEPT(A, x) = YES.
(b) Prove that ACCEPT is undecidable by reducing from HALT.

Problem 3. [30 points] Holiday Migration (2 parts)
Delibird is on her annual holiday migration from Boston to Miami while delivering presents along the U.S.
East Coast. There are n cities along the coast, indexed 1, . . . , n from north to south. City 1 is Boston and
city n is Miami. Delibird can fly south by at most k cities at a time. This means if she’s in city i, she can fly
to city i + j as long as 1 ≤j ≤k and i + j ≤n.

(rounded up). Whenever she arrives in city i, she acquires pi new presents. All pi are non-negative integers.

trip (in Miami) with at least 12 presents. Co

3. Describe how to implement BFS using a QUEUE as the main data structure. Remember that
a QUEUE supports the enqueue and dequeue operations.
Solution: Initialize the queue to contain just the source vertex. Mark the source vertex as
visited. Repeat while the queue is nonempty:
• dequeue the next vertex v.
• For each neighbor u of v, if u is not yet marked as visited, enqueue u and mark it as
visited.
The time complexity of this implementation is also O(|V | + |E|) because we visit every
vertex and check its neighbors once.

citations.snippet:
Problem 3. [30 points] Holiday Migration (2 parts)
Delibird is on her annual holiday migration from Boston to Miami while delivering presents along the U.S.
East Coast. There are n cities along the coast, indexed 1, . . . , n from north to south. City 1 is Boston and
city n is Miami. Delibird can fly south by at most k cities at a time. This means if she’s in city i, she can fly
to city i + j as long as 1 ≤j ≤k and i + j ≤n.
Delibird starts in Boston with 0 presents. Whenever she leaves any city, she gives away half of her presents
(rounded up). Whenever she arrives in city i, she acquires pi new presents. All pi are non-negative integers.
(a) [15 points] Design an O(nk) time DP to determine whether or not it is possible for Delibird to end her
trip (in Miami) with at least 12 presents. Co

6. Binary tree properties
• Binary Search Property: in-order traversal yields the keys in sorted order
• AVL Property: every node’s children have heights that differ by at most 1
• Max-(resp. Min-)Heap Property: every node’s key is no smaller (larger) than those of its children
• An AVL SET satisfies the Binary Search Property and the AVL Property, but (generally) not the
Heap Properties.
• An AVL SEQUENCE satisfies the AVL Property but has no keys, so it doesn’t make sense to talk
about the Binary Search Property or the Heap Properties.
• A HEAP satisfies one of the Heap Properties and the AVL Property (because it is compact), but
(generally) not the Binary Search Property.
• A binary tree could in principle satisfy none of the above properties, e.g. other efficient SE-

Problem 3. [12 points] Pawniard Push (1 part)
Pawniard is navigating a giant n × n chessboard, with squares labeled (x, y) for 0 ≤x, y < n. There is a
known list C of squares that each contain a single coin. Pawniard can move from location (x, y) to:
• (x −1, y + 1) if this square contains a coin
• (x, y + 1) if this square does not contain a coin
• (x + 1, y + 1) if this square contains a coin
Pawniard may start at any square (x, 0) in the back row (all of which contain coins). Design an algorithm
to compute the maximum number of coins that Pawniard can collect before becoming unable to move.
Analyze your algorithm’s runtime. For full credit, your algorithm must run in time O(n2). You need not
prove correctness.

aliases: Storage Restricted Trading Bauble Optimization Technique

– If we buy at least one, we must buy as many as possible
– If we sell at least one, we must sell as many as possible (the entire storage)
– Wait to sell at maximum price in the future
– Buy if pi < pi+1, sell if pi > pi+1
– Only consider selling if there are k baubles in storage

It is also possible to use an AVL set for I instead of a Hash Set. However, this requires more care. Black-box
replacement of the Hash Set with an AVL Set incurs a multiplicative log n runtime overhead for Insert and
Build. Instead, the hats themselves should function as AVL tree nodes and additionally have pointers to their
parents and children in the heaps. This allows the AVL tree to be navigated in constant time instead of using
the Θ(log n) time AVL operations. Augmentations are unaffected because the updates are to data not used
by the AVL tree. BUILD should also Build I out of A before the current step (1). Runtimes for BUILD and
GETMEDIAN are now worst-case, and runtime for INSERT is now only amortized.

Problem 4. [12 points] Heaps (1 part)
Prove or disprove: For every ARRAY A = [a1, a2, . . . , an], if A satisfies the MIN-HEAP Property and the
reverse of A (i.e. [an, an−1, . . . , a1]) satisfies the MAX-HEAP Property, then A is sorted.
Solution:
The claim is false; take as a counterexample A = [1, 3, 2, 4]. MAX-HEAP property requires
A[4] ≥A[3] ≥A[1] and A[4] ≥A[2], which are both satisfied. MIN-HEAP property requires A[1] ≤
A[2] ≤A[4] and A[1] ≤A[3], which are also both satisfied. However, A is not sorted; A[2] = 3 > 2 = A[3].
Common Mistakes:
• Switching Min-Heap and Max-Heap Properties

Problem 4. [16 points] Prismatic Paths (1 part)
Let G = (V, E, w) be a positive-weighted, undirected graph, and let s, t ∈V . Suppose each edge of G has
one of seven colors, and every vertex has exactly one incident edge of each color. Design an O(|V | log |V |)
algorithm to compute the shortest s-t path that contains edges of at least three different colors. Analyze your
algorithm’s runtime and briefly justify correctness.
Solution:
We duplicate G 30 times to keep track of the colors seen so far along a path: the 29 sets of at
most two colors, plus a success state ⋆that collapses all sets of at least three colors. (Note: this could instead
be done with 27 states and a supersink.)

• Given that AVL trees provide insert with worst-case O(log n) and iter ord with

BST and AVL Properties
• Remember: the BST and AVL properties have unrelated functions!
• BST property deals with traversal order.
• AVL property deals with height.
• A binary tree may satisfy both properties, either property alone, or neither!
• One efficient SET implementation is an AVL BST.
• One efficient SEQUENCE implementation is an AVL tree (without the BST property).

Kirby has extended the functionality of a STACK of integers. His MAXSTACK has two additional operations:
• PEEKMAX(): Outputs the maximum value m contained in the MAXSTACK
• POPMAX(): Outputs and removes the maximum value m contained in the MAXSTACK, and addi-

multiple times, this removes the most recent instance of m and everything added after it)

Amortized Analysis
• Operations on Data Structures are not done in a vacuum.
• Usually, a Data Structure supports an algorithm, which uses many operations on the data
structure.
• We don’t care about the worst-case runtime of a single operation. Rather, we care about the
worst-case runtime of a sequence of operations.
• We say that the operations have amortized cost T if any sequence of m operations (starting
from an empty data structure) takes aggregate time at most mT.

Amortized Analysis
• Operations on Data Structures are not done in a vacuum.
• Usually, a Data Structure supports an algorithm, which uses many operations on the data
structure.
• We don’t care about the worst-case runtime of a single operation. Rather, we care about the
worst-case runtime of a sequence of operations.
• We say that the operations have amortized cost T if any sequence of m operations (starting

• Think of amortization like a debit card:
– the true cost of what you buy is what you charge to the card;
– the amortized cost is what you deposit in the bank.
– You can deposit the amount you need immediately before you spend it (no amortiza-

Miskatonic Institute of Technology maintains a line of n watchtowers along the coast that it uses to hold
Cthulhu at Bay. Each tower is identified by a unique rational mile number t. Cultists periodically deactivate
towers, and MIT reactivates them. If enough towers in a row are inactive, Cthulhu will devour the world and
cancel classes.
MIT President Canon Hatebuild wants a database to track the status of the towers. Describe how to use an
AVL tree to implement a database supporting the following worst-case operations:

Toggle the status of the tower with ID t if it exists (i.e. activate an inactive
tower or deactivate an active one) in O(log n) time.
MAXINACTIVESEQ()
Return a maximal count, m, of consecutive inactive towers

prefer three different traversal orders; Ivysaur prefers InOrder traversals, Bulbasaur prefers

PreOrder(T) = T.val, PreOrder(T.left), PreOrder(T.right)
PostOrder(T) = PostOrder(T.left), PostOrder(T.right), T.val

6. Suppose you have some items x, each of which has one comparable key k1(x) and one
hashable key k2(x). Assume that both keys are unique. Describe an unordered SET data
structure that can INSERT efficiently and can FIND or DELETE efficiently using either key.
What is the runtime of each operation, and is it worst-case, amortized, and/or expected?
Solution: This time, we cross-link an AVL tree (keyed by k1) with a hash table (keyed by
k2). Each chain in the hash table will be an linked list (as in the previous exercise) of tree
nodes. FIND by k1 uses one AVL FIND so takes worst-case O(log n) time. FIND by k2 uses
one hash FIND so takes expected O(1) time. INSERT and DELETE use dynamic operations
on both data structures so take amortized and expected O(log n) time.

5. Binary tree properties
• Binary Search Property: in-order traversal yields the keys in sorted order
• AVL Property: every node’s children have heights that differ by at most 1
• Max-(resp. Min-)Heap Property: every node’s key is no smaller (larger) than those of its children
• An AVL SET satisfies the Binary Search Property and the AVL Property, but (generally) not the
Heap Properties.
• An AVL SEQUENCE satisfies the AVL Property but has no keys, so it doesn’t make sense to talk
about the Binary Search Property or the Heap Properties.
• A HEAP satisfies one of the Heap Properties and the AVL Property (because it is compact), but
(generally) not the Binary Search Property.
• A binary tree could in principle satisfy none of the above properties, e.g. other efficient SE-

• Key fact: A tree with the AVL property, is balanced, i.e. h ∈O(log n).
• Proof:
1. Consider any tree with the AVL property with n nodes and height h.
2. Let nh denote that smallest tree one can build with height h and with the AVL property.
3. We have nh ≤n.
4. We show that h ∈O(log nh) ⊆O(log n).
5. As nh−1 > nh−2, to build the smallest tree of height h, we take a smallest tree of height
h −1 as a left subtree and a smallest tree of height h −2 as the right subtree.
6. Therefore, nh ≥nh−1 + nh−2 + 1 (with n0 = 1 and n1 = 2)
7. Trivially nh ≥nh−1 + nh−2 + 1 > 2nh−2, and so nh ∈Ω(2h/2).
8. Hence h ∈O(log nh).

6. Binary tree properties
• Binary Search Property: in-order traversal yields the keys in sorted order
• AVL Property: every node’s children have heights that differ by at most 1
• Max-(resp. Min-)Heap Property: every node’s key is no smaller (larger) than those of its children
• An AVL SET satisfies the Binary Search Property and the AVL Property, but (generally) not the
Heap Properties.
• An AVL SEQUENCE satisfies the AVL Property but has no keys, so it doesn’t make sense to talk
about the Binary Search Property or the Heap Properties.
• A HEAP satisfies one of the Heap Properties and the AVL Property (because it is compact), but
(generally) not the Binary Search Property.
• A binary tree could in principle satisfy none of the above properties, e.g. other efficient SE-

Problem 4. [12 points] Heaps (1 part)
Prove or disprove: For every ARRAY A = [a1, a2, . . . , an], if A satisfies the MIN-HEAP Property and the
reverse of A (i.e. [an, an−1, . . . , a1]) satisfies the MAX-HEAP Property, then A is sorted.
Solution:
The claim is false; take as a counterexample A = [1, 3, 2, 4]. MAX-HEAP property requires
A[4] ≥A[3] ≥A[1] and A[4] ≥A[2], which are both satisfied. MIN-HEAP property requires A[1] ≤
A[2] ≤A[4] and A[1] ≤A[3], which are also both satisfied. However, A is not sorted; A[2] = 3 > 2 = A[3].
Common Mistakes:
• Switching Min-Heap and Max-Heap Properties

citations.snippet:
6.1210 Midterm 1 Practice 1
Name:
10 of 13
Solution: (Dual)
Keep a second AVL TREE SET with the same birds, but keyed by timestamp and augmented with the
minimum ID minID in each subtree. Define recent-up-to(T, max) recursively on this second
tree:
• If T is empty or minID(T) > max: output ⊥.
• If recent-up-to(T.right, max) is not ⊥, output it.
• If T.item has an ID ≤max, output T.item.
• Output recent-up-to(T.left, max).
Common Mistakes:
• Everything from 5(a)
• Traversing the tree
• Assuming (implicitly or explicitly) that ID max is always at the root
• Thinking that recent-up-to(max) is always either recent() or ⊥
• Using recursion instead of recent()
• Using recent() instead of root ID
• Comparing against root timestamp in both recursive cases or neither
• Destroying the tree

2. Recursion
If something has already been defined, do not attempt to redefine it. At best, you gain nothing. You
will, however, lose points based on clarity, concision, ambiguity, or for any mistakes you make. This
is especially important when defining recursive algorithms. Many attempts at
1
def f(x):
2
Base case: return g(x)
3
If b: return f(y)
4

ffeb95e1-67c2-4d1f-b954-8f0970167d63.name: Set of Items Keyed by a Key
ffeb95e1-67c2-4d1f-b954-8f0970167d63.definition: A set S containing items of type X, where each item is associated with an intrinsic key k that uniquely identifies it, and all items and their keys are distinct in S.
aliases: Set of Items Keyed by a Key

citations.snippet:
4. Keys and SETS
If S is a SET of X keyed by k, this means that:
• S mathematically represents a set of items of type X, i.e. all x ∈S are distinct.
• The key k is an intrinsic property of items of type X.
• The keys of all x ∈S are also distinct.
• If the key k is not specified, it is assumed to be the identity function by default, i.e. the key of x
is x itself.
“S is a SET that maps X to Y ” is abuse of notation for “S is a SET of (X, Y ) pairs, keyed by X”,
just as mathematically, a (partial) function S is a set of ordered pairs. If S represents a total function
x 7→x.y, then S does nothing by definition except waste time and space. By contrast, a SET that
represents the function x.y 7→x may be useful.

• S mathematically represents a set of items of type X, i.e. all x ∈S are distinct.

• The keys of all x ∈S are also distinct.
• If the key k is not specified, it is assumed to be the identity function by default, i.e. the key of x
is x itself.

citations.snippet:
4. Multi-sets
Some SET implementations can be adapted naturally to function as multi-sets, where duplicate keys
are allowed, and where find may output any item with the given key. This does not work with HASH
TABLES, which fundamentally rely on distinct keys in a way that other SET implementations we have
seen do not. For e.g. the given solution to #4SUM, if A contains many 0s, it forces H to perform
many repeated FINDS. If instead, H were a multi-set that stored each pair (w, x) separately instead
of counting them, these repeated FINDS would instead be forced collisions, and the expected runtime
analysis of the HASH TABLE no longer works.

citations.snippet:
6. Binary tree properties
• Binary Search Property: in-order traversal yields the keys in sorted order
• AVL Property: every node’s children have heights that differ by at most 1
• Max-(resp. Min-)Heap Property: every node’s key is no smaller (larger) than those of its children
• An AVL SET satisfies the Binary Search Property and the AVL Property, but (generally) not the
Heap Properties.
• An AVL SEQUENCE satisfies the AVL Property but has no keys, so it doesn’t make sense to talk
about the Binary Search Property or the Heap Properties.
• A HEAP satisfies one of the Heap Properties and the AVL Property (because it is compact), but
(generally) not the Binary Search Property.
• A binary tree could in principle satisfy none of the above properties, e.g. other efficient SE-

Three Implementations of the STACK Interface
Linked List
• Pointer-based data structure.
• Each item stored in a node which contains a pointer to the next node below it. Each node
has two fields: node.item and node.next.
• Maintains a pointer to the top node in the STACK (called the head).
• Can insert and delete from the top in Θ(1) time by re-linking pointers.
• Can peek and check emptiness by reading head.
• Therefore, all operations take Θ(1) time.
Array
• Arrays are contiguous chunks of memory cells.
• In addition to the array A, we also maintain a pointer TOP pointing to the first empty cell in
the array. Initially, the TOP pointer is 0.
• To implement push(c), we set A[top]=c and then increment top.
• To implement pop(), we decrement top and then return A[top]

a2d25bff-26f7-42e9-8c68-0b1c488fea6b.name: Intermediate Value Theorem Problem (IVT Problem)
a2d25bff-26f7-42e9-8c68-0b1c488fea6b.definition: A problem where given an array A of length n ≥ 2 such that A[0] ≤ 0 and A[n−1] ≥ 0, the goal is to find an index i such that A[i] × A[i+1] ≤ 0.

Problem 3. [23 points] Individual Value Training (3 parts)
Consider the IVT problem:
• Input: an array A of length n ≥2 such that A[0] ≤0 and A[n −1] ≥0
• Output: an index i such that A[i] × A[i + 1] ≤0
(a) [5 points] Prove that if the input satisfies the given preconditions, then IVT has at least one correct
output.
Solution: (Direct construction)
Let k be the first index such that A[k] ≥0, which exists since A[n −1] ≥0. If k = 0, then A[0] = 0,
so A[0] × A[1] ≤0. If k > 0, then A[k −1] < 0 and A[k] ≥0, so A[k −1] × A[k] ≤0.
Solution: (Induction)
Base case (n = 2) is correct since A[0] ≤0 ≤A[1]. If n > 2, we split into two cases:
• If A[1] ≤0, then A[1 :] is a shorter array that satisfies the precondition, so there exists a correct
output in A[1 :] (and hence in A) by the induction hypoth

same elements except with 2 replaced by 1. However, CLOSEST() should output 2 in

3. Describe a linear time algorithm to sort a set n of strings, each having k English characters.
Solution: Use tuple sort to repeatedly sort the strings by each character from right to left with
counting sort, using the integers {0, . . . , 25} to represent the English alphabet. There are k
rounds of counting sort, and each round takes Θ(n + 26) = Θ(n) time, thus the algorithm
runs in Θ(nk) time. This running time is linear because the input size is Θ(nk).

It is also possible to use an AVL set for I instead of a Hash Set. However, this requires more care. Black-box
replacement of the Hash Set with an AVL Set incurs a multiplicative log n runtime overhead for Insert and
Build. Instead, the hats themselves should function as AVL tree nodes and additionally have pointers to their
parents and children in the heaps. This allows the AVL tree to be navigated in constant time instead of using
the Θ(log n) time AVL operations. Augmentations are unaffected because the updates are to data not used
by the AVL tree. BUILD should also Build I out of A before the current step (1). Runtimes for BUILD and
GETMEDIAN are now worst-case, and runtime for INSERT is now only amortized.

85550037-d355-4b5c-9965-f4ba3d759604.definition: If an array A satisfies A[0] ≤ 0 and A[n-1] ≥ 0, then there exists at least one index i such that A[i] × A[i + 1] ≤ 0.

Problem 3. [23 points] Individual Value Training (3 parts)
Consider the IVT problem:
• Input: an array A of length n ≥2 such that A[0] ≤0 and A[n −1] ≥0
• Output: an index i such that A[i] × A[i + 1] ≤0
(a) [5 points] Prove that if the input satisfies the given preconditions, then IVT has at least one correct
output.
Solution: (Direct construction)
Let k be the first index such that A[k] ≥0, which exists since A[n −1] ≥0. If k = 0, then A[0] = 0,
so A[0] × A[1] ≤0. If k > 0, then A[k −1] < 0 and A[k] ≥0, so A[k −1] × A[k] ≤0.
Solution: (Induction)
Base case (n = 2) is correct since A[0] ≤0 ≤A[1]. If n > 2, we split into two cases:

Problem 1.
Counting Sheep
Mareep is implementing a counter that stores a natural number k (initially 0) in base-n using an
array A of length n. The counter has two operations:
• increment() : increments k by one
• get() : outputs and resets k
Describe how to implement both operations, and prove that they take amortized constant time.
Solution: For increment, we start by incrementing A[0]. Each time A[i] overflows, we reset it
and increment A[i + 1]. If A[n −1] overflows, double n, reallocate A, and set A[n/2] = 1.
For get, output A, reset n = 2, and reallocate A.

2. Modify the Dynamic Array implementation of the SEQUENCE interface such that the opera-
tions insert first and delete first take O(1) amortized time alongside insert last
and delete last.
Solution:
We keep a single array with two pointers, start and end. Whenever we prepend, we move
the start pointer to the left if there is space. Similarly, we move the end pointer to the right
whenever we append. Deletions consist of moving the corresponding pointer in the opposite
direction and can be trivially implemented.
If there is no space for a given insert operation at a time when the array has n elements, we
allocate space such that there will be n free spaces to the left and n to the right of the array.
This ensures that we have enough space for at least n new insertions, which guarantees O(1)

Problem 4. [20 points] Happy Go Lucky (1 part)
Blissey’s Pokémon friends are at integer locations along a line. Blissey is keeping them happy by placing
Lucky Eggs. Each Lucky Egg e is represented as a pair of integers (a, b) with a ≤b, and it makes all
Pokémon at locations x with a ≤x ≤b happy. Blissey’s friends may accidentally break the Lucky Eggs,
which then lose their effect.
Blissey would like to know who is happy. Design a data structure that supports the following operations:
• PLACE(e): Add a Lucky Egg e to the data structure
• BREAK(e): Delete a Lucky Egg e from the data structure
• HAPPY(x): Output TRUE iff the Pokémon at location x is currently happy
Your data structure must use O(n) space, and all operations should have worst-case O(log n) runtime, where

2. Describe how to use a sorted doubly linked list to implement the Set interface. What is the
runtime of each operation?
Solution:
• build sorts the input array in O(n log n) time.
• find min and find max take O(1) time because we have head and tail pointers.
• iter ord scans the list in order in O(n) time.
• find, find next, and find prev require scanning through the list, and so take
O(n) time.
• insert and delete also require scanning through the list to find the right spot, and
is O(n) time.

citations.snippet:
4. Keys and SETS
If S is a SET of X keyed by k, this means that:
• S mathematically represents a set of items of type X, i.e. all x ∈S are distinct.
• The key k is an intrinsic property of items of type X.
• The keys of all x ∈S are also distinct.
• If the key k is not specified, it is assumed to be the identity function by default, i.e. the key of x
is x itself.
“S is a SET that maps X to Y ” is abuse of notation for “S is a SET of (X, Y ) pairs, keyed by X”,
just as mathematically, a (partial) function S is a set of ordered pairs. If S represents a total function
x 7→x.y, then S does nothing by definition except waste time and space. By contrast, a SET that
represents the function x.y 7→x may be useful.

TABLE could have forced collisions, and the expected runtime analysis no longer works.

6. Binary tree properties
• Binary Search Property: in-order traversal yields the keys in sorted order
• AVL Property: every node’s children have heights that differ by at most 1
• Max-(resp. Min-)Heap Property: every node’s key is no smaller (larger) than those of its children
• An AVL SET satisfies the Binary Search Property and the AVL Property, but (generally) not the
Heap Properties.
• An AVL SEQUENCE satisfies the AVL Property but has no keys, so it doesn’t make sense to talk
about the Binary Search Property or the Heap Properties.
• A HEAP satisfies one of the Heap Properties and the AVL Property (because it is compact), but

citations.snippet:
Problem 5. [12 points] Josephus’ Problem (2 parts)
The Josephus Problem is defined as follows: There are n people arranged on a circle and we are given
a number m ≤n. Starting with a designated first person, we proceed around the circle removing every
mth person. This process continues until everyone has been removed. The order in which the people are
removed is called the (n, m) Josephus Permutation of the set {1, . . . , n}. For example, the (5, 2) Josephus
Permutation is [2, 4, 1, 5, 3].
(a) [5 points] Assuming that m is a constant (that is, m = O(1)), which of the following data structures
would best help you output the (n, m) Josephus Permutation in O(n) time? Make a choice, and very
briefly justify your answer. No credit will be given for answers without any justification.

Solution: T(n) = Θ(n) by the substitution method. We want to prove T(n) ≤cn, so
assume it is true for values smaller than n. Substituting that in we have:
T(n) ≤cn/5 + 7cn/10 + n
T(n) ≤9cn/10 + n
We set this equal to cn = 9cn/10+n and solve for c = 10. Therefore T(n) ≤cn for c ≥10

Mareep is implementing a counter that stores a natural number k (initially 0) in base-n using an

■Decreases greatly whenever an expensive operation is called.
Solution:
The fake cost is c′ = c + ∆Φ which we want to show is O(f). That means when c is
expensive, we need Φ to drop in order to make c′ = O(f). When c is cheap, increases in Φ are probably
fine, but it is not essential since if Φ drops it is even better (though Φ should gradually increase in order
to still obey the lower bound when there is an expensive operation in the future). Finally, Φ needs a
constant lower bound: Say we proved c′ = c+∆Φ = O(f) always, then P c+Φn−Φ0 = O(nf), and
thus (P c)/n = O(f) −Φn/n. If Φn were extremely negative (say −2nfn), then (P c)/n = Ω(2nf)
instead of O(f)!

Problem 5. [12 points] Josephus’ Problem (2 parts)
The Josephus Problem is defined as follows: There are n people arranged on a circle and we are given
a number m ≤n. Starting with a designated first person, we proceed around the circle removing every
mth person. This process continues until everyone has been removed. The order in which the people are
removed is called the (n, m) Josephus Permutation of the set {1, . . . , n}. For example, the (5, 2) Josephus
Permutation is [2, 4, 1, 5, 3].

6.1210 Midterm 1 Review
Name:
10 of 11
Solution: (Dual)
Keep a second AVL TREE SET with the same birds, but keyed by timestamp and augmented with the
minimum ID minID in each subtree. Define recent-up-to(T, max) recursively on this second
tree:
• If T is empty or minID(T) > max: output ⊥.
• If recent-up-to(T.right, max) is not ⊥, output it.
• If T.item has an ID ≤max, output T.item.
• Output recent-up-to(T.left, max).
Common Mistakes:
• Everything from 6(a)
• Traversing the tree
• Assuming (implicitly or explicitly) that ID max is always at the root
• Thinking that recent-up-to(max) is always either recent() or ⊥
• Using recursion instead of recent()
• Using recent() instead of root ID
• Comparing against root timestamp in both recursive cases or neither
• Destroying the tree

The Robot Coin Collector problem is set up as follows:
The problem consists of a n × n grid indexed by (i, j) for i, j = 1, . . . , n. The point (1, 1) is at the bottom

coin in (i, j) or 0 if there is no coin at the grid point.
We want to know what is the maximum value of the coins that a robot, starting in (1, 1), can collect, if it can
only go either RIGHT or UP.

6.1210 Midterm 2 Review
Name:
4 of 8
(h) [3 points] If G is a binary tree, then the finishing order of DFS (starting from the root and processing
children from left to right) is always the same as:
□The PRE-ORDER traversal
□The IN-ORDER traversal
■The POST-ORDER traversal
□Neither
Solution:
A DFS will finish its out-going edges first, then finish the current node. As there are no cycles, the left
sub-tree will finish before the right sub-tree is visited. After the right sub-tree is finished, the root is
finished.

Problem 4. [15 points] Road Trip (1 part)
Off you go to the long awaited road trip across the country from Boston to San Fransisco. To make the trip
a bit more fun, you and your buddy Chucky decide to play a game. In each city you stay at, one will pay
the other an amount of money equal to the number of M’s Donots locations in the city (the newest craze in

once you arrive in San Fransisco, the game terminates (you don’t leave again even if you arrived before 100
nights)

1051e54d-6ccb-4119-b477-78dbfc960c77.name: Robot Coin Collector Problem
1051e54d-6ccb-4119-b477-78dbfc960c77.definition: A pathfinding problem where a robot moves on an n × n grid from (1,1) to (n,n), collecting coins with values at grid points, moving only right or up, and the goal is to maximize the sum of collected coin values.

citations.snippet:
Problem 5. [16 points] Robot Coin Collector (2 parts)
The Robot Coin Collector problem is set up as follows:
The problem consists of a n × n grid indexed by (i, j) for i, j = 1, . . . , n. The point (1, 1) is at the bottom
left corner, and the point (n, n) is at the top right corner. There are coins with positive values in some grid
points. The value of the coins in each grid point is stored in a matrix C. Assume that Ci,j is the value of the
coin in (i, j) or 0 if there is no coin at the grid point.
We want to know what is the maximum value of the coins that a robot, starting in (1, 1), can collect, if it can
only go either RIGHT or UP.
For this problem, we always prefer a faster algorithm to a slower one. Faster algorithms will get more credit
than slower ones.

The Robot Coin Collector problem is set up as follows:
The problem consists of a n × n grid indexed by (i, j) for i, j = 1, . . . , n. The point (1, 1) is at the bottom
left corner, and the point (n, n) is at the top right corner. There are coins with positive values in some grid
points. The value of the coins in each grid point is stored in a matrix C. Assume that Ci,j is the value of the
coin in (i, j) or 0 if there is no coin at the grid point.
We want to know what is the maximum value of the coins that a robot, starting in (1, 1), can collect, if it can
only go either RIGHT or UP.
For this problem, we always prefer a faster algorithm to a slower one. Faster algorithms will get more credit
than slower ones.

(d) [3 points] If A ≤p B and there is an algorithm for A that runs in polynomial time, then there is an
algorithm for B that runs in polynomial time.
□TRUE
■FALSE
Solution:
We can only infer that if B is solvable in polynomial time, then A is too, but not the converse. B could
be a way harder problem than A. For example, let B be an extremely hard decision problem of which
we know an easy YES-input y and an easy NO-input x. Then A could just be any polynomial-time
solvable decision problem (say s-t REACHABILITY), and the ‘transformation’ of inputs (that shows
A ≤p B) is one that takes inputs in A, solves A by itself, and outputs y if the answer is supposed to be
yes, or x otherwise.

4 of 8
(h) [3 points] If G is a binary tree, then the finishing order of DFS (starting from the root and processing
children from left to right) is always the same as:
□The PRE-ORDER traversal
□The IN-ORDER traversal
■The POST-ORDER traversal
□Neither
Solution:
A DFS will finish its out-going edges first, then finish the current node. As there are no cycles, the left
sub-tree will finish before the right sub-tree is visited. After the right sub-tree is finished, the root is
finished.

GR which is identical to G but with all the edges reversed. Solve for both an adjacency list

Solution: First we describe how to construct the adjacency representation of GR given that
of G. We loop through each vertex v in G. For each neighbor u of v, we add v to the list of
neighbors of u in GR. This takes O(|V | + |E|) time.
For adjacency matrices, the adjacency matrix for GR is simply the transpose of the adjacency
matrix for G. It takes O(|V |2) time to construct the transpose because you need to go through
all O(|V |2) entries in the matrix.

3. Describe how to implement BFS using a QUEUE as the main data structure. Remember that
a QUEUE supports the enqueue and dequeue operations.
Solution: Initialize the queue to contain just the source vertex. Mark the source vertex as
visited. Repeat while the queue is nonempty:
• dequeue the next vertex v.
• For each neighbor u of v, if u is not yet marked as visited, enqueue u and mark it as
visited.
The time complexity of this implementation is also O(|V | + |E|) because we visit every
vertex and check its neighbors once.

Lecture 12: Reductions
• Notation: if there is a reduction that transforms A to B (a reduction from A to B), we say
A ≤B, or A reduces to B
• Think of the ≤as a comparison of hardness: A is no harder than B because solving B gives
a solution to A as well
• Very useful when dealing with hard problems
• Neither problem need be solved nor even solvable!

Many-One Reductions
• A Many-One Reduction from a problem A to a problem B is a function (algorithm) f with
the property that A = B ◦f
• A many-one reduction is a Turing reduction with the restriction that the subroutine for B can
be used only once, at the end, and the answer must be returned without modification
• Think: take an input x for A, transform it using f into an input y = f(x) for B, and then
compute B(y), which should give the same answer as A(x)
• Sometimes called mapping reduction

3. For each vertex (v, s, r) with r > 0, add a directed edge to (v, s, r−1) with cost 1 to represent Wingull
resting in place.
Next, we expand G into an unweighted graph G′ by unrolling any swimming edge of cost t(u, v) > 1
into a chain of t(u, v) unit-cost edges. Observe that Wingull can always choose to wait and fly instead
of swimming for excessively long durations. Specifically, from state (u, su, ru), Wingull can always reach
(v, sv, rv) by waiting ru ≤67 minutes at u, flying from u to v in 1 minute, and resting 67−rv ≤67 minutes
at v. This alternative path takes at most 67 + 1 + 67 = 135 minutes. Thus, we can ignore any swimming
edge with cost t(u, v) > 135 when constructing G′ since it wll never be optimal to take that edge.
Let s be the starting node Slateport. A successful mission

Let G = (V, E, w) be a positive-weighted, undirected graph, and let s, t ∈V . Suppose each edge of G has
one of seven colors, and every vertex has exactly one incident edge of each color. Design an O(|V | log |V |)
algorithm to compute the shortest s-t path that contains edges of at least three different colors. Analyze your
algorithm’s runtime and briefly justify correctness.

2. In a graph G = (V, E) with positive edge weights, there are special nodes, s1, s2, . . . , sk,
where k is not necessarily a constant. For every node v in the graph, we want to find the
distance from the closest special node to v. Describe a O(|E| + |V | log |V |) algorithm to do
so.
Solution: We add a so-called “supernode” s∗as another vertex to G. We connect s∗to each
of s1, s2, . . . , sk with an edge of weight 0. This effectively forces the shortest path (or any
other path for that matter) from s∗to v to start at a special node. In addition, setting the edge
weights to 0 means that the shortest distance from s∗to v will be equal to the shortest of the
distances from s1, s2, . . . , sk to v. Hence, we can just run Dijkstra from s∗and output the
shortest path distances between s∗and v

Problem 4. [15 points] Jack’s Tea (1 part)
Commodore Jack is an honest tea merchant. He has a map of the Caribbean with n port cities and O(n2)
one-way sea routes between them. Every time one of Jack’s ships enters a port p, it must pay a tax of t(p)
doubloons (even if it is only passing through p). Every time one of Jack’s ships sails the route (p1, p2), it
can collect d(p1, p2) doubloons in generous donations from Jack’s less-well-armed competitors. Jack wants
to pick a home port h. Each month, he will send a ship of tea from h to every port in the Caribbean and
back. He would like to pick h so as to minimize the total net cost in doubloons that his fleet must pay.2 Give
an O(n3) time algorithm to help Jack pick h, and analyze its runtime. You need not prove correctness.

longer path would have to pass through a vertex that is not between u and v in the topological order, so
would have an edge that violates the order.

are semi-connected.

• The weight w(π) of a path π in a weighted graph is the sum of edge weights along π
• The (weighted) shortest path from s ∈V to t ∈V is path of minimum weight from s to t

• The infimum of a set is the greatest lower bound, which is the largest number that is less than
or equal to every element in the set. The infimum does not have to be a member of the set
itself.
• (Generalizes edge-count distance in unweighted graphs)

– We have an Optimal Subproblem Property: Subpaths of shortest paths are shortest paths

one-way sea routes between them. Every time one of Jack’s ships enters a port p, it must pay a tax of t(p)

• The infimum of a set is the greatest lower bound, which is the largest number that is less than
or equal to every element in the set. The infimum does not have to be a member of the set
itself.
• (Generalizes edge-count distance in unweighted graphs)

– δ(s, t) = ∞if no path from s to t.
– We have an Optimal Subproblem Property: Subpaths of shortest paths are shortest paths
(or else could splice in a shorter path)

one-way sea routes between them. Every time one of Jack’s ships enters a port p, it must pay a tax of t(p)
doubloons (even if it is only passing through p). Every time one of Jack’s ships sails the route (p1, p2), it
can collect d(p1, p2) doubloons in generous donations from Jack’s less-well-armed competitors. Jack wants
to pick a home port h. Each month, he will send a ship of tea from h to every port in the Caribbean and
back. He would like to pick h so as to minimize the total net cost in doubloons that his fleet must pay.2 Give
an O(n3) time algorithm to help Jack pick h, and analyze its runtime. You need not prove correctness.
Solution:

Problem 5. [30 points] Mod (2 parts)
In each of the following, let G = (V, E) be an undirected graph with integer weights, and let s, t ∈V . You
must analyze runtime, but you need not prove correctness.
(a) [15 points] Give an O(|V ||E|) time algorithm that outputs the smallest integer multiple of 6121 that
is the weight of some s-t path (or state that none exists).
Solution:
• Create G′ = (V ′, E′), where
– V ′ = V × Z6121
– E′ = {(ux, vx+w(u,v)) : (u, v) ∈E, x ∈Z6121}
– w′(ux, vy) = w(u, v)
• BF in G′ to compute and output δ(s0, t0)
Runtime: G′ is larger than G by a factor of 6121 (constant), so graph construction takes linear time.
BF runtime is still O(|V ||E|). Total is O(|V ||E|).
Correctness (not required) follows from the 1-1 correspondence between s-v paths of weight x in G
and s0

Problem 6. [18 points] Single Source Second-Shortest Paths (1 part)
Let G = (V, E, w) be a directed graph with non-negative edge weights. For vertices s, t ∈V , define the
second-shortest distance ∆(s, t) to be minimal such that:
• ∆(s, t) > δ(s, t)
• ∆(s, t) is the length of some s-t path
If every s-t path is a shortest path (and in particular, if δ(s, t) = ∞), then ∆(s, t) = ∞. Design an algorithm
that takes as input G and vertices s and t, and computes ∆(s, t). Analyze your algorithm’s runtime. For full
credit, it should run in time O(|V | log |V | + |E|). You need not prove correctness.
Hint: How can you track whether a path has deviated from all shortest paths?

Problem 2. [12 points] Bisharp’s Opening (1 part)
Bisharp is navigating a giant n × n chessboard, with squares labeled (x, y) for 0 ≤x, y < n. Bisharp can
move from any square (x, y) to any of the four diagonally adjacent squares (x ± 1, y ± 1). There is a known
list C of squares that each contain a single coin. There is also a known list K of squares (disjoint from C)
that each contain a Kingambit. Bisharp may start anywhere and can make any number of moves, but can
never occupy the same square as a Kingambit or leave the chessboard. Design an algorithm to compute the
maximum number of coins that Bisharp can collect. Analyze runtime and briefly justify correctness. For
full credit, your algorithm must run in time O(n2).
Note: each coin may be collected only once, no matter how many time B

Problem 3. [12 points] Pawniard Push (1 part)
Pawniard is navigating a giant n × n chessboard, with squares labeled (x, y) for 0 ≤x, y < n. There is a
known list C of squares that each contain a single coin. Pawniard can move from location (x, y) to:

• (x + 1, y + 1) if this square contains a coin

to compute the maximum number of coins that Pawniard can collect before becoming unable to move.

prove correctness.

citations.snippet:
Problem 6. [18 points] Single Source Second-Shortest Paths (1 part)
Let G = (V, E, w) be a directed graph with non-negative edge weights. For vertices s, t ∈V , define the
second-shortest distance ∆(s, t) to be minimal such that:
• ∆(s, t) > δ(s, t)
• ∆(s, t) is the length of some s-t path
If every s-t path is a shortest path (and in particular, if δ(s, t) = ∞), then ∆(s, t) = ∞. Design an algorithm
that takes as input G and vertices s and t, and computes ∆(s, t). Analyze your algorithm’s runtime. For full
credit, it should run in time O(|V | log |V | + |E|). You need not prove correctness.
Hint: How can you track whether a path has deviated from all shortest paths?

Bisharp is navigating a giant n × n chessboard, with squares labeled (x, y) for 0 ≤x, y < n. Bisharp can

Common Mistakes:
• Conceptual misunderstandings (that typically did not lose points if otherwise correct):
– Not seeing that graph can be undirected
– Not seeing or using general properties of undirected graphs (derived from symmetric edges):
* CCs = SCCs = W(eakly)CCs
* Full BFS/DFS = Kosaraju-Sharir
* In particular, there are no edges between SCCs: condensation graph has only “islands”
• Mistakes in algorithm (that lost points):
– 7 points max: Only do one BFS/DFS, assuming there’s a fixed starting point as input (or otherwise
not knowing the difference between full BFS/DFS and single-source BFS/DFS)
* No runtime points: Not trivial that extending this to all starting points remains as efficient
– 7 points max: Assume there can only be a constant

Problem 3. [12 points] Pawniard Push (1 part)
Pawniard is navigating a giant n × n chessboard, with squares labeled (x, y) for 0 ≤x, y < n. There is a
known list C of squares that each contain a single coin. Pawniard can move from location (x, y) to:
• (x −1, y + 1) if this square contains a coin
• (x, y + 1) if this square does not contain a coin
• (x + 1, y + 1) if this square contains a coin
Pawniard may start at any square (x, 0) in the back row (all of which contain coins). Design an algorithm
to compute the maximum number of coins that Pawniard can collect before becoming unable to move.
Analyze your algorithm’s runtime. For full credit, your algorithm must run in time O(n2). You need not
prove correctness.

3baa2467-d32b-4c3d-a4ac-bbc8b1e62279.definition: Finding the shortest path between vertices s and t in a colored, positive-weighted undirected graph where the path contains edges of at least three distinct colors.

citations.snippet:
Problem 4. [16 points] Prismatic Paths (1 part)
Let G = (V, E, w) be a positive-weighted, undirected graph, and let s, t ∈V . Suppose each edge of G has
one of seven colors, and every vertex has exactly one incident edge of each color. Design an O(|V | log |V |)
algorithm to compute the shortest s-t path that contains edges of at least three different colors. Analyze your
algorithm’s runtime and briefly justify correctness.
Solution:
We duplicate G 30 times to keep track of the colors seen so far along a path: the 29 sets of at
most two colors, plus a success state ⋆that collapses all sets of at least three colors. (Note: this could instead
be done with 27 states and a supersink.)

Lecture 15: Bellman-Ford
Weighted Paths
• The weight w(π) of a path π in a weighted graph is the sum of edge weights along π
• The (weighted) shortest path from s ∈V to t ∈V is path of minimum weight from s to t
• δ(s, t) = inf{w(π) | π is an s-t path} is the distance (or shortest-path weight) from s to t
• The infimum of a set is the greatest lower bound, which is the largest number that is less than
or equal to every element in the set. The infimum does not have to be a member of the set
itself.
• (Generalizes edge-count distance in unweighted graphs)
• As with unweighted graphs:
– δ(s, t) = ∞if no path from s to t.
– We have an Optimal Subproblem Property: Subpaths of shortest paths are shortest paths
(or else could splice in a shorter path)
• Why infimum instead of minimum? Even in f

Course Information
9
Regrade requests. If you feel that a midterm or final exam was not graded properly, you may
submit a regrade request. The request must be made online by the announced deadline, typically
one week after grades are released. The request should include a detailed explanation of why you
believe that the original grader made an error. Regrade requests are not for disputing the rubric,
questioning value judgments, requesting explanations, or pleading for leniency. Please make sure
you read the solutions carefully before requesting a regrade. For any regrade request, we reserve
the right to regrade the entire assignment, and your grade may be adjusted up or down as a result
of the regrade. We will dismiss summarily any request that does not follow these directions.

Lecture 1: Introduction and Integer Arithmetic
3
– Have to read the input: For each input digit d ∈{x0, . . . , xn−1, y0, . . . , yn−1}, if we
had a purported addition algorithm which never does a basic operation involving d,
then there would be two possible inputs to the algorithm, x, y and x′, y′, which would
give the same output but for which x + y̸ = x′ + y′ – we could build such inputs by
changing the digit d. So, the algorithm would be incorrect.
– Have to write the output: At the end of the algorithm we have to output an n + 1-digit
number. We didn’t count the “return” as a basic operation, but writing the output to e.g.
standard out is going to require n operations.
• From the perspective of this course, this closes the story for addition: we have an algo-
rithm using O(n) basic op

10410d34-1c88-4c6c-869b-fbfb65b15183.name: Problem Simplification in Algorithm Design
10410d34-1c88-4c6c-869b-fbfb65b15183.definition: The technique of reducing a complex problem to a simpler version that is still unsolved and working on that simpler problem to make progress towards solving the original.

citations.snippet:
10
Lecture 1: Introduction and Integer Arithmetic
– Simplify the problem: find a simpler version of the problem which you still can’t solve
and work on that. When you solve it, you’ve made progress towards the harder version
you started with. (Can’t solve the simpler version? Simplify again!)
– Take a break. For most people, it’s not helpful to sit and stare at the problem – if you
have been working fruitlessly – thinking the same thought over and over – for a long
time (perhaps 30 minutes), it’s often best to break the cycle and try something else.
Algorithmic ideas sometimes need to percolate in your subconscious mind for a while.
It’s common to struggle with a problem, give up, go to bed, and have a solution form
the next morning in the shower.

Lecture 2: Efficient Algorithms
Just as an algorithm is a mathematical abstraction of a computer program,
a model of computation is a mathematical abstraction of a computer.
Models of computation: What is an “operation?”
We defined worst-case runtime in terms of the number of “operations” an algorithm takes to do its
job. But what counts as an “operation?”
To answer this question, we have to define a model of computation. Just as a computer specifies
a set of basic operations programs on it can execute, a model of computation specifies what basic
operations algorithms written in this model can execute.
And just as there are many different kinds of computer, there are many different useful models
of computation:

• Decidable (L24)
A decision problem P (or its language) is decidable if there is an algorithm A such that
A(x) = YES ⇐⇒P(x) = YES,
and
A always halts,
i.e. A returns YES on all YES-inputs, and returns NO on all NO-inputs. We say that A
computes P, and that A is a decider (an algorithm that halts).

• Recognizable (R24)
A decision problem P (or its language) is recognizable if there is an algorithm A such that
A(x) = YES ⇐⇒P(x) = YES,
i.e. A returns YES on all YES-inputs, but either returns NO or loops forever on NO-inputs.
An algorithm is correct when it gives a correct answer for every possible input.
An algorithm is efficient if it uses few resources: running time, memory, etc.

d13b0790-0a14-4080-a382-a1261fa67776.name: Linked List Implementation of Stack
d13b0790-0a14-4080-a382-a1261fa67776.definition: A pointer-based data structure for stacks where each node contains an item and a pointer to the next node below it, maintaining a head pointer to the top of the stack allowing Θ(1) time insertion and deletion at the top.

citations.snippet:
2
Lecture 3: Sequences
Three Implementations of the STACK Interface
Linked List
• Pointer-based data structure.
• Each item stored in a node which contains a pointer to the next node below it. Each node
has two fields: node.item and node.next.
• Maintains a pointer to the top node in the STACK (called the head).
• Can insert and delete from the top in Θ(1) time by re-linking pointers.
• Can peek and check emptiness by reading head.
• Therefore, all operations take Θ(1) time.
Array
• Arrays are contiguous chunks of memory cells.
• In addition to the array A, we also maintain a pointer TOP pointing to the first empty cell in
the array. Initially, the TOP pointer is 0.
• To implement push(c), we set A[top]=c and then increment top.
• To implement pop(), we decrement top and then return A[top]

2. Modify the Dynamic Array implementation of the SEQUENCE interface such that the opera-
tions insert first and delete first take O(1) amortized time alongside insert last
and delete last.
Solution:
We keep a single array with two pointers, start and end. Whenever we prepend, we move
the start pointer to the left if there is space. Similarly, we move the end pointer to the right
whenever we append. Deletions consist of moving the corresponding pointer in the opposite
direction and can be trivially implemented.
If there is no space for a given insert operation at a time when the array has n elements, we
allocate space such that there will be n free spaces to the left and n to the right of the array.
This ensures that we have enough space for at least n new insertions, which guarantees O(1)

5. Given an unweighted graph G = (V, E) in which some edges are red and some are blue, find
a path from s to t with the minimal number of red edges.
Solution: We combine BFS and DFS. The main idea is that using a DEQUE, we can BFS
w.r.t. red edges while simultaneously condensing blue edges using DFS.
• Initialize a DEQUE Q = [s], d(s) = 0, and P(s) = ⊥
• While Q is non-empty:
– Remove the first element u from Q
– For each unvisited out-neighbor v of u:
* set P(v) = u
* if (u, v) is red, set d(v) = d(u) + 1 and append v to Q
* if (u, v) is blue, instead set d(v) = d(u) and prepend v to Q
• Follow parent pointers from t and output the resulting path
Correctness and runtime proofs are as DFS and BFS.

5. Given an unweighted graph G = (V, E) in which some edges are red and some are blue, find

Lecture 6: Hashing
• Today, we are going to talk about HASHING.
• Hashing is one of the most powerful algorithmic tools out there.
• Many of the ideas we have seen so far (array, binary search, merge sort) are concepts that
apply in the non-computer setting: e.g., sorting a stack of exams by last name.
• Hash tables are different: they take full advantage of the fact that computers can do things
quickly/cheaply that humans cannot.
• If you are stranded on a desert island with only one data structure, you probably would want
to be stranded with a hash table.

• Recall that the Set interface stores a set of items

e294c218-9812-4fa7-a081-0951a4a745af.definition: The problem of arranging elements of an array into a sorted order based on a key comparison.

3

• Even though insertions are more costly, a typical use case prefers the cheap find(key)
provided by the sorted array. YMMV.

Sorting Problem
• Input: (static) array A of n numbers. More generally, we allow items with keys that can be
compared. (E.g. students in 6.1210, keyed by name. Keys are compared lexicographically.)
• Output: (static) array B which is a sorted permutation of A
– Permutation: array with same elements in a different order
– Sorted: B[i −1] ≤B[i] for all i ∈{1, . . . , n −1}
• Example: [8, 2, 4, 9, 3] 7→[2, 3, 4, 8, 9]
• A sort is in place if it uses O(1) ext

• insert last analysis:
– Base case: if i = 0, array is a singleton so is sorted.
– Induction: assume correctness for i. If A[i] >= A[i - 1], array is sorted. Other-
wise, swapping last two elements maintains precondition on A[:i-1] and allows us to
sort A[:i] by induction. At this point, A[i] >= A[i - 1], so array is sorted.
– Runtime: S(1) ∈Θ(1) and S(i) ∈S(i −1) + O(1).
* Expand shorthand: Take c s.t. S(1) ≤c and S(i) −S(i −1) ≤c.
* Substitution: S(i) ≤ci, so S(i) ∈O(i).
Base case: by construction
Induction: S(i) ≤S(i −1) + c ≤c(i −1) + c = ci.

• insert last analysis:
– Base case: if i = 0, array is a singleton so is sorted.
– Induction: assume correctness for i. If A[i] >= A[i - 1], array is sorted. Other-
wise, swapping last two elements maintains precondition on A[:i-1] and allows us to
sort A[:i] by induction. At this point, A[i] >= A[i - 1], so array is sorted.
– Runtime: S(1) ∈Θ(1) and S(i) ∈S(i −1) + O(1).

midpoint between the two subarrays. Let us modify the construction: let jmidpoint = ⌊m/2⌋, and
let the left subarray be A[:, 0 : jmidpoint], and the right subarray be A[:, jmidpoint + 1 : m], so that
column jmidpoint does not lie in either subarray. We will now determine whether a peak lies in the
left subarray, the midpoint column, or the right subarray, as follows.

do). Check if A[i∗, jmidpoint] is a peak in A. If it is, return (i∗, jmidpoint).
• If not: then A[i∗, jmidpoint] must have a neighbor that is strictly greater than it. This neighbor
cannot lie along the midpoint column

Review: Binary Search
• Input: (static) array A of n numbers in non-decreasing order, and a target number t.
• Output: number of indices i such that A[i] < t.
• Example: [2, 3, 4, 8, 9], 5 7→3
• Brute force algorithm (iterating over the entire array) takes Θ(n) time, but we can do better
with divide and conquer!
• Divide and conquer algorithm: recursively divide the array in half, and search only one half.
– Base case: if A is empty, output 0.
– Recursive step: compare t and A[m], where m := ⌊n/2⌋.
* If t ≤A[m], search prefix A[: m] for t and output the result.
* If A[m] < t, search suffix A[m + 1 :] for t, add m + 1, and output the sum.
• Corre

Review: Binary Search
• Input: (static) array A of n numbers in non-decreasing order, and a target number t.
• Output: number of indices i such that A[i] < t.
• Example: [2, 3, 4, 8, 9], 5 7→3
• Brute force algorithm (iterating over the entire array) takes Θ(n) time, but we can do better
with divide and conquer!
• Divide and conquer algorithm: recursively divide the array in half, and search only one half.
– Base case: if A is empty, output 0.
– Recursive step: compare t and A[m], where m := ⌊n/2⌋.
* If t ≤A[m], search prefix A[: m] for t and output the result.
* If A[m] < t, search suffix A[m + 1 :] for t, add m + 1, and output the sum.
• Corre

citations.snippet:
4. Describe a linear time algorithm to sort n integers from the range [−n49, . . . , n50].
Solution: We can add n49 to each number so integers are all non-negative. After this, all
the keys are < 2n50 < n51 and so we can apply Radix sort with base n. Afterward, we can
subtract n49 from each element of the output and get the correct sorted order.

Given an unsorted array A = [a0, . . . , an−1] containing n positive integers, the DUPLICATES prob-
lem asks whether there is an integer that appears more than once in A (the answer is ‘yes’ or ‘no’;
you don’t need to return the repeated integer). All of the questions in this section should have 1-3
sentence answers.

Open Addressing (Not examined!)
Open addressing is a different way of dealing with collisions. Whereas in chaining we use auxiliary
data structures to deal with collisions, in open addressing collisions are stored in the hash table
itself!
Different open addressing schemes are defined by different probing strategies. A probing strategy
dictates which slot to try next if the particular slot being looked at is occupied with a different key.

Assuming that the probing scheme function ℎcan be evaluated in 𝑂(1) time and that probing
sequences are random, open addressing has similar asymptotic performance to chaining, with some
increased efficiency especially for small load factors. In practice common probing schemes are:
• Linear probing: ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = (ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖) mod 𝑚where ℎ′ is a regular hash function.
• Quadratic probing: ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = (ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖2) mod 𝑚can help to “spread out” the collisions in
the table.
• Double hashing (usually better than linear or quadratic): ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖· ℎ′′(𝑘), where
ℎ′, ℎ′′ are distinct hash functions.
Stay tuned in 6.1220 (and/or read the CLRS textbook) for more detailed analysis of hashing, open
addressing, probing schemes, and more.

Running time analysis:
• find(k):
– Compute h(k) – let’s assume that this takes Θ(1) time
– Get pointer to start of chain c = A[h(k)] – one lookup
– Run c.find(k) – Θ(L) amortized time, if chain has length L and is stored in a dynamic array.
• Total time: Θ(1 + L).

3b800269-3789-4a0c-b02a-aeaee834334d.name: Probing Scheme
3b800269-3789-4a0c-b02a-aeaee834334d.definition: A function that defines which slot to try next when a collision occurs in open addressing hashing.

citations.snippet:
Lecture 6: Hashing
9
Open Addressing (Not examined!)
Open addressing is a different way of dealing with collisions. Whereas in chaining we use auxiliary
data structures to deal with collisions, in open addressing collisions are stored in the hash table
itself!
Different open addressing schemes are defined by different probing strategies. A probing strategy
dictates which slot to try next if the particular slot being looked at is occupied with a different key.
Mathematically, an open addressing hashing scheme is defined by a function (the probing scheme)
ℎ: U × {0, . . . , 𝑚−1} ↦→{0, . . . , 𝑚−1}
For a given key 𝑘, we first attempt to store 𝑘in ℎ(𝑘, 0), if occupied, we try ℎ(𝑘, 1), then ℎ(𝑘, 2)
and so on. See Figure ??.

Assuming that the probing scheme function ℎcan be evaluated in 𝑂(1) time and that probing
sequences are random, open addressing has similar asymptotic performance to chaining, with some
increased efficiency especially for small load factors. In practice common probing schemes are:
• Linear probing: ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = (ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖) mod 𝑚where ℎ′ is a regular hash function.
• Quadratic probing: ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = (ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖2) mod 𝑚can help to “spread out” the collisions in
the table.
• Double hashing (usually better than linear or quadratic): ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖· ℎ′′(𝑘), where
ℎ′, ℎ′′ are distinct hash functions.
Stay tuned in 6.1220 (and/or read the CLRS textbook) for more detailed analysis of hashing, open
addressing, probing schemes, and more.

5e605495-4312-4fbb-aa97-5bf87dc94c79.name: Quadratic Probing
5e605495-4312-4fbb-aa97-5bf87dc94c79.definition: A probing scheme in open addressing using the function ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = (ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖^2) mod 𝑚, which helps spread out collisions in the hash table.

Assuming that the probing scheme function ℎcan be evaluated in 𝑂(1) time and that probing
sequences are random, open addressing has similar asymptotic performance to chaining, with some
increased efficiency especially for small load factors. In practice common probing schemes are:
• Linear probing: ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = (ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖) mod 𝑚where ℎ′ is a regular hash function.
• Quadratic probing: ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = (ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖2) mod 𝑚can help to “spread out” the collisions in
the table.
• Double hashing (usually better than linear or quadratic): ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖· ℎ′′(𝑘), where
ℎ′, ℎ′′ are distinct hash functions.
Stay tuned in 6.1220 (and/or read the CLRS textbook) for more detailed analysis of hashing, open
addressing, probing schemes, and more.

6. Let x and y be nodes in a BST, and suppose y is the successor of x and x has no right child.
Prove that y is an ancestor of x, and in particular x is in the left subtree of y.
Solution:
Let y be the successor of x and let z be the least common ancestor of x and y.
If z = y, then y is an ancestor of x. If z = x, since x has no right subtree, y must be in its
left subtree, so y ≤x which is impossible. Otherwise, x and y are in different subtrees of
z, which means z is between x and y, contradicting that y is the successor of x. The only
possible case is the first one, where y is the least common ancestor. Since x ≤y and y is an
ancestor of x, x must be in the left subtree of y.

6. Let x and y be nodes in a BST, and suppose y is the successor of x and x has no right child.
Prove that y is an ancestor of x, and in particular x is in the left subtree of y.
Solution:
Let y be the successor of x and let z be the least common ancestor of x and y.

ancestor of x, x must be in the left subtree of y.

• Key fact: A tree with the AVL property, is balanced, i.e. h ∈O(log n).
• Proof:
1. Consider any tree with the AVL property with n nodes and height h.
2. Let nh denote that smallest tree one can build with height h and with the AVL property.
3. We have nh ≤n.
4. We show that h ∈O(log nh) ⊆O(log n).
5. As nh−1 > nh−2, to build the smallest tree of height h, we take a smallest tree of height
h −1 as a left subtree and a smallest tree of height h −2 as the right subtree.
6. Therefore, nh ≥nh−1 + nh−2 + 1 (with n0 = 1 and n1 = 2)
7. Trivially nh ≥nh−1 + nh−2 + 1 > 2nh−2, and so nh ∈Ω(2h/2).
8. Hence h ∈O(log nh).

• Remember: the BST and AVL properties have unrelated functions!
• BST property deals with traversal order.

Theorem 1. Let f be a field that augments an AVL tree T of n nodes, and suppose that the contents
