including f(x.left)) and f(x.right)) in constant time. Then, we can maintain the values
of f in all nodes of T during insertion and deletion without asymptotically affecting the O(lg n)
performance of these operations.
The main idea of the proof is that a change to an f field in a node x only propagates to the
ancestors of x in the tree. That is, changing f(x) may require f(x.parent) t

Neighbor Sets/Adjacencies
• The outgoing neighbor set of u ∈V is Adj+(u) = {v ∈V | (u, v) ∈E}
• The incoming neighbor set of u ∈V is Adj−(u) = {v ∈V | (v, u) ∈E}
• The out-degree of a vertex u ∈V is deg+(u) = |Adj+(u)|

2. Given a directed graph G, construct and analyze the runtime of an algorithm to create graph
GR which is identical to G but with all the edges reversed. Solve for both an adjacency list
and adjacency matrix representation.
Solution: First we describe how to construct the adjacency representation of GR given that
of G. We loop through each vertex v in G. For each neighbor u of v, we add v to the list of
neighbors of u in GR. This takes O(|V | + |E|) time.
For adjacency matrices, the adjacency matrix for GR is simply the transpose of the adjacency
matrix for G. It takes O(|V |2) time to construct the transpose because you need to go through
all O(|V |2) entries in the matrix.
Both runtimes are linear.

citations.snippet:
4
Lecture 10: Graph Search
Shortest Paths Tree
• How to return a shortest path from source vertex s for every vertex in graph?
• Many paths could have length Ω(|V |), so returning every path could require Ω(|V |2) time
• Instead, for all v ∈V , store its parent P(v): second to last vertex on a shortest path from s
• Let P(s) be null (no second to last vertex on shortest path from s to s)
• Set of parents comprise a shortest paths tree with O(|V |) size!
(i.e., reversed shortest paths back to s from every vertex reachable from s)

• (If no path from s to v, do not store v in P and set δ(s, v) to ∞)

The Relaxation Framework
• Before addressing the key question, need some scaffolding.
• Searching for shortest paths from s, our shortest path algorithms will maintain a state: a set
of “distance estimates” – numbers d(v) for each vertex v.
• We will maintain the crucial invariant that d(v) is ∞or the weight of a path from s to v. In
particular, d ≥δ pointwise.
• At end of algorithm, goal is that d(v) = δ(v).
• As with BFS, you can also use parent pointers to represent a shortest path tree.
• Key subroutine: edge relaxation.
– Based on Triangle Inequality: δ(a, c) ≤δ(a, b) + δ(b, c)1

fe531c87-42ad-4606-9618-7aa01dca2f57.definition: Proof that DFS visits every vertex reachable from the start vertex and correctly assigns predecessor pointers, using induction on distances from the start vertex.

citations.snippet:
6
Lecture 10: Graph Search
Correctness
• Claim: DFS visits v and correctly sets P(v) for every vertex v reachable from s
• Proof: induct on k, for claim on only vertices within distance k from s
– Base case (k = 0): P(s) is set correctly for s and s is visited
– Inductive step: Consider vertex v with δ(s, v) = k′ + 1
– Consider vertex u, the second to last vertex on some shortest path from s to v
– By induction, since δ(s, u) = k′, DFS visits u and sets P(u) correctly
– While visiting u, DFS considers v ∈Adj(u)
– Either v is in P, so has already been visited, or v will be visited while visiting u
– In either case, v will be visited by DFS and will be added correctly to P
Running Time
• Algorithm visits each vertex u at most once and spends O(1) time for each v ∈Adj(u)
• Work upper bounded

4. Describe how to implement DFS using a STACK as the main data structure. Remember that
a STACK supports the push and pop operations.
Solution:
Initialize the Stack to contain just the source vertex. Repeat while the stack is
nonempty:

Lecture 11: Connected components
Definition 1. In an undirected graph G, two vertices u, v are in the same connected compo-
nent if there is a u–v path in G.
Fact. The connected components containing u and v are either identical or disjoint.
Proof. Consider two cases:
– There is a u–v path: Every vertex reachable from u is also reachable from v (and vice
versa).
– There is no u–v path: No vertex reachable from u is reachable from v.
(Otherwise, there would be a u–v path through this vertex.)
Finding connected components
• By running an algorithm for single-source reachability (i.e., BFS or DFS) on every vertex in
a graph, we can find all of its connected components in linear time.

c99fe12a-5e50-4621-bae1-eb181dad497d.definition: A directed graph admits a topological ordering if and only if it is a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

citations.snippet:
Lecture 11: Connected components
9
• Topological order: A topological order of a directed graph G = (V, E) is an ordering
N : V →{1, 2, . . . , |V |} on the vertices such that: every edge (u, v) ∈E satisfies N(u) <
N(v).
– Why is this useful? As one example, if the graph G represents software dependencies,
the topological ordering gives you an order in which to install software packages such
that every package is installed before its dependencies.
• Exercise: Prove that a directed graph admits a topological ordering if and only if it is a DAG.
• How to find a topological order?
• Claim: If G = (V, E) is a DAG, the reverse of a finishing order is a topological order
• Proof: Need to prove, for every edge (u, v) ∈E that u is ordered before v,
i.e., the visit to v finishes before visiting u.

• Today: use reductions to simplify algorithm design and analysis

Many-One Reductions
• A Many-One Reduction from a problem A to a problem B is a function (algorithm) f with
the property that A = B ◦f
• A many-one reduction is a Turing reduction with the restriction that the subroutine for B can
be used only once, at the end, and the answer must be returned without modification
• Think: take an input x for A, transform it using f into an input y = f(x) for B, and then
compute B(y), which should give the same answer as A(x)
• Sometimes called mapping reduction
• Write A ≤m B

5b9f26ac-8c3d-4cea-a8b4-c7d6ac4e53c0.definition: The output of the Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP) problem can be represented either as the distance function δ(s, -) or as a shortest path tree P.

citations.snippet:
Lecture 12: Reductions
5
Output form
• The output of SSSP can be assumed to take one of two forms
1. the distance function δ(s, −)
2. the shortest path tree P
• Each output form can be reduced to the other
– 1 →2: For every vertex v, δ(s, v) is its depth in P, computed with a pre-order traversal
– 2 →1: For each vertex v, set P(v) to be any in-neighbor u with δ(s, v) = 1 + δ(s, u)
• When solving SSSP, you can put the output in either form
• When using SSSP, you can assume that you have either or both output forms
• We will encounter many problems where parent pointers behave similarly; you need not
track them explicitly when solving a problem, but you may still use them when helpful
• Similarly: DFS tree, start and finish times, edge classifications

also have indices that are smaller than j’s children, and i’s parent’s index is smaller than j’s

citations.snippet:

Lecture 15: Bellman-Ford
Weighted Paths
• The weight w(π) of a path π in a weighted graph is the sum of edge weights along π
• The (weighted) shortest path from s ∈V to t ∈V is path of minimum weight from s to t
• δ(s, t) = inf{w(π) | π is an s-t path} is the distance (or shortest-path weight) from s to t
• The infimum of a set is the greatest lower bound, which is the largest number that is less than
or equal to every element in the set. The infimum does not have to be a member of the set
itself.
• (Generalizes edge-count distance in unweighted graphs)
• As with unweighted graphs:

(or else could splice in a shorter path)

6ec0e228-3410-448b-b1a7-94e2cdf06964.definition: A framework in shortest path algorithms maintaining distance estimates d(v) for each vertex v that are always greater than or equal to the shortest path distances δ(v) and updated via edge relaxations.

citations.snippet:
Lecture 14: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
3
The Relaxation Framework
• Before addressing the key question, need some scaffolding.
• Searching for shortest paths from s, our shortest path algorithms will maintain a state: a set
of “distance estimates” – numbers d(v) for each vertex v.

Lecture 14: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
5
* Relaxation can only decrease estimates d(v)
* Relaxation is safe, i.e., maintains that each d(v) is weight of a path to v (or ∞)
– Suffices to show d(v) = δ(v) when vertex v is removed from Q
* Proof by strong induction on number k of vertices removed from Q
* Base Case (k = 1): s is first vertex, and d(s) = 0 = δ(s) by non-negativity
* Inductive Step: Suppose we are removing v from Q, and that for all vertices u
already removed from Q, d(u) = δ(u).
* Let π be a shortest path from s to v (so w(π) = δ(v))
* Let y be the first vertex in π still in Q (possibly v itself), and let x be its predecessor
in π.
* When x was removed from Q, d(x) = δ(x) by induction, so:
d(y) ≤d(x) + w(x, y)
(x, y) was relaxed when x was removed
= δ(y)

Lecture 15: Bellman-Ford
Weighted Paths
• The weight w(π) of a path π in a weighted graph is the sum of edge weights along π
• The (weighted) shortest path from s ∈V to t ∈V is path of minimum weight from s to t
• δ(s, t) = inf{w(π) | π is an s-t path} is the distance (or shortest-path weight) from s to t
• The infimum of a set is the greatest lower bound, which is the largest number that is less than
or equal to every element in the set. The infimum does not have to be a member of the set
itself.
• (Generalizes edge-count distance in unweighted graphs)
• As with unweighted graphs:
– δ(s, t) = ∞if no path from s to t.
– We have an Optimal Subproblem Property: Subpaths of shortest paths are shortest paths
(or else could splice in a shorter path)
• Why infimum instead of minimum? Even in f

• The infimum of a set is the greatest lower bound, which is the largest number that is less than
or equal to every element in the set. The infimum does not have to be a member of the set
itself.
• (Generalizes edge-count distance in unweighted graphs)
• As with unweighted graphs:
– δ(s, t) = ∞if no path from s to t.
– We have an Optimal Subproblem Property: Subpaths of shortest paths are shortest paths
(or else could splice in a shorter path)

2b213715-50bf-4cfe-84cd-4bc4adf8d9ee.name: Shortest path with negative-weight cycle
2b213715-50bf-4cfe-84cd-4bc4adf8d9ee.definition: A shortest path of length |V| in graph G that contains a negative-weight cycle, indicating no well-defined shortest path exists with fewer vertices.

citations.snippet:
8
Lecture 15: Bellman-Ford
Extras: Return Negative-Weight Cycle or Space Optimization
• Claim 5: Shortest s0 −v|V | path π for any witness v contains a negative-weight cycle in G
• Proof: Since π contains |V | + 1 vertices, must contain at least one cycle C in G
– C has negative weight (otherwise, remove C to make path π′ with fewer vertices and
w(π′) ≤w(π), contradicting witness v)
• Can use just O(|V |) space by storing only δ(s0, vk−1) and δ(s0, vk) for each k from 1 to |V |
• Traditionally, Bellman-Ford stores only one value per vertex, attempting to relax every edge
in |V | rounds; but estimates do not correspond to k-Edge Distances, so analysis trickier
• But these space optimizations don’t return a negative weight cycle

ac582188-3aa5-4414-a6c5-0e7ef4cdcdf3.name: Usefulness of All-Pairs Shortest Paths
ac582188-3aa5-4414-a6c5-0e7ef4cdcdf3.definition: Reasons why APSP is studied including practical querying over large networks and its equivalences to other problems.

citations.snippet:
2
Lecture 16: All Pairs Shortest Paths
Why study all-pairs shortest paths?
Reason 1: It is useful in its own right.
• If you run a large network (communication, transport, etc.) you might want to compute all
shortest paths at once up front so that you can quickly answer shortest-path queries later on.
Reason 2: Fast algorithms for APSP give fast algorithms for many other problems.
• Virginia Vassilevska Williams and Ryan Williams showed (2010) that APSP is equivalent, in
a certain formal sense, to a number of other problems:
– Finding negative triangles in a graph
– Finding the minimum-weight cycle in a graph (with non-negative edge weights)
– The replacement-paths problem (find a path from here to there avoiding all edges on the
shortest path).
– . . .

Reason 1: It is useful in its own right.
• If you run a large network (communication, transport, etc.) you might want to compute all
shortest paths at once up front so that you can quickly answer shortest-path queries later on.
Reason 2: Fast algorithms for APSP give fast algorithms for many other problems.
• Virginia Vassilevska Williams and Ryan Williams showed (2010) that APSP is equivalent, in
a certain formal sense, to a number of other problems:
– Finding negative triangles in a graph
– Finding the minimum-weight cycle in a graph (with non-negative edge weights)
– The replacement-paths problem (find a path from here to there avoiding all edges on the
shortest path).
– . . .
Why negative edge weights?
Some appl

Algorithms for APSP
• General directed graph, negative weights: The best known algorithms for arbitrary graphs all take |𝑉|3−𝑜(1) = |𝑉|3/(small) time.
• General directed graph, non-negative weights: Running Dĳkstra from every node achieves 𝑂(|𝑉|2 log |𝑉| + |𝑉| · |𝐸|).
A major open question is whether an |𝑉|2.9999-time algorithm is possible.

Today: Johnson’s Algorithm for APSP
• Goal: Match the cost of running time of Dĳkstra from every node.
• Running time: 𝑂(|𝑉|2 log |𝑉| + |𝑉| · |𝐸|).
• Handles the most serious case (WOW!):
– Directed graphs
– Weighted
– With negative weights
The plan
1. Look for negative-weight cycles.
• If you find them, output FAIL.
• Using Bellman-Ford, this takes 𝑂(|𝑉| · |𝐸|) time.
• A more sophisticated version of the algorithm can compute APSP on rest of the graph.
(Hint: Decompose into strongly connected components using Kosaraju-Sharir.)
2. Make all edge weights non-negative, with a careful reweighting.
• This reweighting must preserve the shortest paths.
• Tool: Clever use of Bellman-Ford.
• This again takes 𝑂(|𝑉| · |𝐸|) time.
3. Run the naïve Dĳkstra-from-eve

A reweighting that preserves shortest paths
• We will construct a reweighting that preserves the shortest path between any two vertices.
• Let 𝜙: 𝑉→Z be some function.
• Key Idea: For every vertex 𝑣∈𝑉:
– Add 𝜙(𝑣) to all outgoing edges of 𝑣.
– Subtract 𝜙(𝑣) from all incoming edges to 𝑣.
– This transformation preserves the weight of every path through 𝑣!

• Claim: This transformation increases the weight of any (𝑢, 𝑣) path by 𝜙(𝑢) −𝜙(𝑣).

ff786afa-3116-4b4a-b336-4a7e802713ba.name: Handling Negative Cycles in APSP
ff786afa-3116-4b4a-b336-4a7e802713ba.definition: A technique to compute shortest paths in graphs that may contain negative weight cycles by identifying strongly connected components (SCCs) with negative cycles and adjusting shortest path computations accordingly.
aliases: Negative Cycle Handling in All Pairs Shortest Paths

Lecture 16: All Pairs Shortest Paths
Johnson’s Algorithm: Handling Negative-Weight Cycles
Note: The following material was not covered in lecture. Instead, you will practice it on the pest.
Handling Negative Cycles
• As with SSSP, even if 𝐺has negative cycles, some shortest paths may exist
• How can we modify Johnson to compute these shortest paths?
• First: for which pairs 𝑢, 𝑣are 𝛿(𝑢, 𝑣) = −∞?
• Recall: 𝛿(𝑠, 𝑡) = −∞iff some 𝑠-𝑡path contains a vertex on a negative cycle
• Negative cycles must be within a strongly connected component
• Idea: Compute SCCs, check for negative cycles within SCCs, then compute reachability
• Compute SCCs of 𝐺and condensation graph 𝐻(Kosaraju)
• Identify the SCCs containing negative cycles (Bellman-Ford)

– δ(s, t) = ∞if no path from s to t
– We have an Optimal Subproblem Property: Subpaths of shortest paths are shortest paths

1. Round i of Bellman-Ford
Let G be a weighted graph with vertices s and v, and assume there is a shortest path from
s to v that uses at most i edges. Prove that when running Bellman-Ford, after relaxing the
edges into the ith layer of the duplicated graph, the shortest distance to v is already known.
Solution: After relaxing the edges into the ith layer, Bellman-Ford has computed δ(s0, vi)
(in the notation from lecture). We must prove that δ(s0, vi) = δ(s, v); that’s what we mean
by the shortest distance being known at the ith layer.
We use strong induction on i. For i = 0, the only vertex with a shortest path from s traversing
at most zero edges is vertex s, and Bellman-Ford correctly sets δ(s0, s0) = 0 = δ(s, s)
without relaxing any edges.
Now suppose the claim is true for all vertices

Greedy Choice Property
• Shortest Paths algorithms used the Optimal Sub-Problem Property: An optimal solution to a

• With Greedy Algorithms, we can make the decision to solve the problem locally, without the
need to solve the sub-problems first. So a Greedy Algorithm is an iterative algorithm that
makes locally optimal choices one by one.

decision (the “greedy choice”) can always be extended into a globally optimal solution.

3. Inductive Step: Let’s prove that the greedy algorithm, GREEDY , is optimal for
n leftovers. First, let’s prove that we can schedule the leftovers at times ≤n −1.
Assume the optimal solution is S. If all the leftovers in S are scheduled to be eaten
at times ≤n −1, then we’re done. Otherwise, there’s at least one leftover, L that
expires at time t ≥n. With our induction hypothesis, we know that the remaining
leftovers can be scheduled at times ≤n−2, so we can schedule L at time n−1. As
a result, WLOG, all expiration times are ≤n. By GCP we can assume the optimal
solution S contains the greedy choice, and so does GREEDY . Therefore, we can
reduce the problem size and using induction, we can claim that the GREEDY
algorithm was not worse than the optimal S.

number of bits possible.
• The input symbols come from an alphabet of n symbols.
E.g., Alphabet is {A, B, C, D, . . . , Z}.
• We assume that the sender and receiver both know how often each symbol occurs.
E.g., in English text A appears 8.2% of the time, B appears 1.5% of the time, etc.
• A simple way to send symbols over the wire is to map each symbol to a ⌈log2 n⌉-bi

• Let’s recap the steps that lead us to the pure Dynamic Programming solution:
1. Recognize the recursive nature of the problem.

(c) Understand how the solution depends on the set of decisions possible plus the corresponding recursive calls.

• Input: an array A denoting the values of the coins.
S Let M(i) be the maximum value of coins we can pick from A[i :], for i ∈{0, . . . , n −1}.
R M(i) = max{M(i + 1), A[i] + M(i + 2)}, for i = {0, . . . , n −1}.
T Each M(i) depends on M(i′) with larger index i′ > i. Therefore, we can compute M(i) in
decreasing order of i.
B M(i) = 0 if i ≥n (i.e. if A[i :] is empty).
O Output is M(0). Note, however, that we may want the actual list of coins, which we will
discuss next.
T There are n values M(i). Each takes O(1) to compute for a total of O(n).

allowed).

Proving Correctness: The Optimal Substructure Property for LCS
• Why could we use DP?
• How do we argue correctness?
• Recall that we came up with the recursive algorithm using the fact that optimal solutions
contain optimal solutions to subproblems.
1. Any optimal solution S that picks A[0] and B[0] (when A[0] = B[0]) also contains an
optimal solution for the subproblem defined by A[1 :] and B[1 :].
2. Any optimal solution S that does not pick A[0] contains an optimal solution for the
subproblem defined by A[1 :] and B.
3. Any optimal solution S that does not pick B[0] contains an optimal solution for the
subproblem defined by A and B[1 :].
• However, the Optimal Substructure Property (OSSP) is the opposite: optimal solutions to
subproblems extend to optimal solutions

Proving Correctness: The Optimal Substructure Property for LCS
• Why could we use DP?
• How do we argue correctness?
• Recall that we came up with the recursive algorithm using the fact that optimal solutions
contain optimal solutions to subproblems.
1. Any optimal solution S that picks A[0] and B[0] (when A[0] = B[0]) also contains an
optimal solution for the subproblem defined by A[1 :] and B[1 :].
2. Any optimal solution S that does not pick A[0] contains an optimal solution for the
subproblem defined by A[1 :] and B.
3. Any optimal solution S that does not pick B[0] contains an optimal solution for the
subproblem defined by A and B[1 :].
• However, the Optimal Substructure Property (OSSP) is the opposite: optimal solutions to
subproblems extend to optimal solutions

The Row Coin Problem as SSSP
• Many problems usually solved using DP can also be modeled as SSSP.
• The resulting graph is closely related to the dependency graph of the DP table.

lem dependencies, and weights the value obtained by making choices. Just as in the depen-
dency graph, edges that “skip” subproblems represent the constraint that no two consecutive
coins can be picked.

Lecture 20: DP II
8
Efficiency Tradeoff: S vs. R
• In our DP for LIS, we enforced the monotonicity constraint by increasing the number of
subproblems.
• This isn’t necessary; we could instead constrain the subproblems and put the work of en-
forcement into the relate step.
S Let M(i) be the length of the longest increasing subsequence of A[i :] that begins with
A[i], where 0 ≤i < |A|.
R M(i) = 1 + max {M(j) : j > i and A[j] > A[i]}
T Increasing order of i.
B None.
O Output is max M.
T M has n entries. Each entry takes O(n) to compute. Computing the output takes O(n)
time. Total is O(n2).
• In our previous DPs, the runtime analysis was always tight. We always used all of our memo
entries, and each took Θ(1) time to compute. This is not true for the above DP!
• Can we make R more efficient?

c461986e-cdce-4c8f-b834-723de0836db5.name: Largest Sum Contiguous Subarray Problem
c461986e-cdce-4c8f-b834-723de0836db5.definition: The problem of finding the contiguous subarray within a one-dimensional array of numbers which has the largest sum.

citations.snippet:
Lecture 20: DP II
9
Exercise: You are given an array A of n integers.
1. Describe and analyze and algorithm to compute the largest sum of a contiguous subarray of
A.
2. (Challenging) Describe and analyze and algorithm to compute the largest product of a con-
tiguous subarray of A.
For example, if A = [−6, 12, −7, 0, 14, −7, 5], then the first algorithm should return 12 + (−7) +
0 + 14 = 19 while the second should return (−6) ∗12 ∗(−7) = 504.
Both algorithms should run in time O(n). Assume that all arithmetic operations take O(1) time.
Hint: Keep a state variable to denote whether you have started the subarray or not.
Hint: For problem 2, what other information do you need to keep from your past choices?

SSSP for General Graphs
• The problem is how to handle cycles.
• If we don’t have negative cycles, then all shortest paths are simple paths, and therefore they
don’t repeat nodes.
• The idea is to use some of the tricks we learned in L19-20. In particular, we will “remember”
how many edges we have used so far.
• This way, our table of subproblems will not have cycles, even if the graph G does.

Lecture 22: DP IV: Subset Sum and Pseudopolynomial Time
3
Is Our Subset Sum Algorithm Polynomial Time?
• Input size is n + 1: one integer L and n integers in A
• Is O(nL) bounded above by a polynomial in n + 1? NO, not necessarily
• On w-bit word RAM, L ≤2w and w ≥lg(n + 1), but we don’t have an upper bound on w
• E.g., w = n is not unreasonable, but then running time is O(n2n), which is exponential
Pseudopolynomial
• Algorithm runs in pseudopolynomial time: running time is bounded above by a constant-
degree polynomial in input size and input integers
• Such algorithms are polynomial in the case that integers are polynomially bounded in input
size, i.e., nO(1) (same case that Radix Sort runs in O(n) time)
• Counting sort O(n + u), radix sort O(n logn u), direct-access array build O(n + u)

cb24c16f-9901-471b-b4d4-f9591adc93d1.name: Partition Problem
cb24c16f-9901-471b-b4d4-f9591adc93d1.definition: Determine if a set of n positive integers can be split into two subsets having equal sums.

citations.snippet:
1. Describe an algorithm to solve Partition: Given a set of n positive integers A, determine
whether A can be partitioned into two subsets A1 and A2 of equal sum.
For example, A = {1, 3, 4, 12, 19, 21, 22} can be partitioned into A1 = {1, 19, 21} and
A2 = {3, 4, 12, 22}, which both have sum 41.
Solution: Let S be the sum of all the number in A. In any partition, P A1 + P A2 = S.
That means P A1 = P A2 if and only if P A1 = S/2. So the problem is equivalent to
looking for a subset of A with sum S/2, so we can solve it by running the algorithm for
Subset Sum on A with T = S/2.

Lecture 23: Complexity
• Usually problems of these other types can be reduced to decision problems!
– Problem A reduces to problem B if the ability to solve B (efficiently) gives you the
ability to solve A (efficiently).
– Johnson’s algorithm for APSP is an example of a reduction: APSP to SSSP.
– Ex: reduce optimization (find the length of the longest increasing subsequence) to
decision (given a target length L, does there exist an increasing subsequence of length
at least L) using binary search.

Lecture 23: Complexity
5
• If we ever find a poly-time algorithm for any NP-complete problem, it would yield a poly-
time algorithm for all problems in NP.
• Contrapositive: if P̸ = NP, then any NP-complete problem cannot have a poly-time algo-
rithm.
• The punchline: many different NP-complete problems known including subset sum, longest
simple path, 3-colorability, and 3SAT! In decades, no efficient algorithm found for any of
them. Therefore, all are very likely to not have efficient algorithms.
• What if P = NP? A world where brute-force search is unnecessary and creativity can be
automated!
– Could find proof of any true mathematical statement (which has a polynomial-size
proof) in polynomial time – no more need for 6.1210 lecturers!
– Public-key cryptography would be impossible!

– Then we claim that H computes HALT correctly:
* P(x) halts
=⇒
Q outputs YES always
=⇒
EQUIV(Q, R) = YES.
* P(x) doesn’t halt
=⇒
Q loops
=⇒
EQUIV(Q, R) = NO.
Undecidability in unexpected places
Of course, these are thinly veiled disguises of HALT, so perhaps do not really answer the question.
More interesting are problems like the following:
• Does a multivariate polynomial equation with integer coefficients have an integer solution?
Example: 16x2 + 7y3 + z = 0. See Hilbert’s Tenth Problem and the MRDP Theorem.
• Given a string s and length ℓ, is there a program of length ≤ℓthat prints s?
(e.g. the string 00000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000 has the much
shorter description “50 0s”).
See Kolmogor

There are also remarkable connections between computability the-
ory and other areas of math and computer science. For instance, Anand, along with Ji, Vidick,

entangled particles can interact with a polynomial-time algorithm by sending polynomial-length

Problem 3.
Asymptotics
(a) Asymptotic addition
Prove or disprove: if f1 ∈O(f2) and g1 ∈O(g2), then f1 + g1 ∈O(f2 + g2).
Solution:
From the definition, we can find constants cf, Nf, cg, Ng such that for
all n ≥Nf, f1(n) ≤cf · f2(n), and for all n ≥Ng, g1(n) ≤cg · g2(n). Take
c = max(cf, cg) and N = max(Nf, Ng). Then for all n ≥N, f1(n) + g1(n) ≤
cf·f2(n)+cg·g2(n) ≤c·f2(n)+c·g2(n) ≤c·(f2(n)+g2(n)). Thus f1+g1 ∈O(f2+g2).
Rubric:
• Correct answer
• Apply definition to preconditions
• Find c, N
• Verify definition for conclusion

Problem 3.
Tofu Sammich Game
Snom gave her tofu sandwich to Ditto and Psyduck, who now want to divide it up between them.
There are n sections (numbered from 0 on the left to n −1 on the right). Each section has tastiness
ti ∈Z.
Ditto and Psyduck take turns doing one of the following:

• Cut the sandwich into two parts each with a positive integer number of sections, eat the left

Ditto wants to maximize D and Psyduck wants to maximize P.

Solution: D = (D + P) + (D −P)

11095d89-8b43-42a7-be41-324f58ac8f4a.name: 3-Coloring Problem
11095d89-8b43-42a7-be41-324f58ac8f4a.definition: Given a graph G=(V,E), decide if there exists a function ϕ: V→{r,g,b} such that adjacent vertices have different colors.

citations.snippet:
Problem 1.
Hardness
Recall that 3COLOR, defined below, is NP-complete.
Input: an undirected graph G = (V, E)
Output: YES iff G admits a proper 3-coloring, i.e. a function ϕ : V →{r, g, b} such that for
every {u, v} ∈E, ϕ(u)̸ = ϕ(v)
(a) Define the EXACT BOOLEAN COVER problem as follows:
Input: a collection S of subsets of a universe U
Output: YES iff there exists a subset T ⊆S that partitions U
Prove that the following is a reduction from 3COLOR to EBC:
Input: G = (V, E)
Let U = V ∪(E × {r, g, b})
For each v ∈V, c ∈{r, g, b}, include in S a set Sv,c = {v}∪{(e, c) : v ∈e ∈E}
For each e ∈E, c ∈{r, g, b}, include in S the set {(e, c)}
Output: (S, U)
Solution: Suppose G has a 3-coloring ϕ. Then let T include:
• Sv,ϕ(v) for each v ∈V :
• {(e, c)} for each e = {u, v} ∈E, where c̸ ∈{ϕ(u), ϕ(v)}
Ea

citations.snippet:
Problem 2.
Recognizability
Let L be a decision language. Prove that L is decidable iff both L and its complement L are
recognizable.
Solution: The forward direction is easy; a decider for L is also a recognizer for L, and flipping
its output produces a decider (and hence recognizer) for L.
Conversely, suppose L and its complement are both recognizable, say by algorithms A and B
respectively. We decide L as follows:
•Input is x
•Run A(x) and B(x) in parallel
•If A(x) says YES, output YES
•If B(x) says YES, output NO
L and L partition all inputs, so one of A(x) or B(x) outputs YES. The above algorithm is therefore
a decider. It outputs YES iff A does, so it decides L.

Problem 3.
Diagonalization
(a) Give a concrete, computable function f such that for every polynomial time algorithm
B, for cofinitely many inputs x, B(x) halts in at most (not asymptotically) f(|x|) time.
Solution: Many functions will work, e.g. f(n) = 2n.
(b) Construct (with proof) a decider A such that for every polynomial time algorithm B,
for infinitely many inputs x, we have A(x)̸ = B(x). You may assume a computable
bijection ϕ that maps strings to pairs of strings.
Solution: Define A as follows:
Input is x
Let (B, y) = ϕ(x)
Run B for f(|x|) steps on input x
Return the opposite result (or if B(x) hasn’t terminated yet, output YES)
This algorithm always halts (in exponential time with f(n) = 2n), so is a decider.

136b881d-90cc-4847-84b6-34035dab1b56.name: Parallel Simulation
136b881d-90cc-4847-84b6-34035dab1b56.definition: Running two algorithms simultaneously on the same input to combine their outputs for decision-making.

citations.snippet:
Problem 2.
Recognizability
Let L be a decision language. Prove that L is decidable iff both L and its complement L are
recognizable.
Solution: The forward direction is easy; a decider for L is also a recognizer for L, and flipping
its output produces a decider (and hence recognizer) for L.
Conversely, suppose L and its complement are both recognizable, say by algorithms A and B
respectively. We decide L as follows:
•Input is x
•Run A(x) and B(x) in parallel
•If A(x) says YES, output YES
•If B(x) says YES, output NO
L and L partition all inputs, so one of A(x) or B(x) outputs YES. The above algorithm is therefore
a decider. It outputs YES iff A does, so it decides L.

B, for cofinitely many inputs x, B(x) halts in at most (not asymptotically) f(|x|) time.

Prove or disprove: if f1 ∈O(f2) and g1 ∈O(g2), then f1 + g1 ∈O(f2 + g2).

5. Find and analyze a more efficient algorithm for the inversion count problem.
Solution: We will use Divide & Conquer in a way similar to Merge Sort. We divide the
array into two equal halves. The main observation is that an inversion is one of 2 types:
(1) “intra-half” where both indices come from the same half; or (2) “inter-half” where each
index comes from a different half. We count the intra-half inversions by invoking the algo-
rithm recursively in each half. We count the inter-half inversions with a procedure similar to
the“merge” step in Merge Sort.

Problem 2.
Rocket Recruits
Giovanni has recruited n new Grunts for Team Rocket. For each i ∈{0, . . . , n −1}, Grunt i has
ki Pok´emon. All of the ki are positive and distinct.
Giovanni wants to pair them into teams with exactly p Pok´emon between them. A pair of Grunts
(x, y), with x < y, such that kx + ky = p is called a battle pair.
Giovanni wants to find two quantities: the number B of battle pairs he can make, and the battle
pair (x∗, y∗) for which x∗is minimal.1
(a) Describe an algorithm to find B and (x∗, y∗) with a worst-case runtime of O(n log n).
Prove your algorithm correct, and analyze its runtime.
(b) Describe an algorithm to find B and (x∗, y∗) with an expected runtime of O(n). Prove
your algorithm correct, and analyze its runtime.

Bulbasaur, Ivysaur and Venusaur are exploring a Binary Tree. However, for Binary Trees they
prefer three different traversal orders; Ivysaur prefers InOrder traversals, Bulbasaur prefers

Problem 3.
Long Jump
Henry is unsatisfied with the current long jump rules and wants to give athletes prizes according
to his own set of rules. He arrives at the competition with a bag full of Snickers bars to give the
athletes. Whenever he’s feeling generous, he selects a minimum distance threshold t. An athlete is
eligible to receive this prize if their most recent jump was at least distance t. He gives the prize to
the eligible athlete who jumped most recently, or to Srini if no athlete is eligible. Athletes have no
limits to their number of attempts.
Henry needs a data structure that can support the following operations:
• JUMP(a, d): Record that an athlete with the name a just achieved a long jump distance of d
• PRIZE(t): Output the name of the prize winner, given distance threshold

Problem 2.
Nesting
Klefki wants to store a SET of locks. Each lock x has two keys: a comparable key k1(x) and a
hashable key k2(x). The ordered pair (k1(x), k2(x)) is a unique identifier, but neither key need in-
dividually be unique. Help Klefki implement a SET data structure in which the FIND and DELETE
operations can take keys from either or both key spaces. (If FIND is given only one type of key, it
can return any lock with that key. If DELETE is given only one type of key, it should delete every
lock with the given key.) All three operations should run in O(log n) time. Analyze the runtime of
each, including classifying each as worst-case, amortized, and/or expected. Prove tighter bounds
when possible.
Solution: Keep two nested data structures. The first is an AVL set A, keyed by k1.

hashable key k2(x). Assume that both keys are unique. Describe an unordered SET data
structure that can INSERT efficiently and can FIND or DELETE efficiently using either key.
What is the runtime of each operation, and is it worst-case, amortized, and/or expected?
Solution: This time, we cross-link an AVL tree (keyed by k1) with a hash table (keyed by
k2). Each chain in the hash table will be an linked list (as in the previous exercise) of tree
nodes. FIND by k1 uses one AVL FIND so takes worst-case O(log n) time. FIND by k2 uses
one hash FIND so takes expected O(1) time. INSERT and DELETE use dynamic operations
on both data structures so take amortized and expected O(log n) time.

consisting of a set L of locations (including rooms, hallways, staircases, and elevators) and a set

pass the door in either direction. For each key type t, Liza knows a set of locations Lt ⊆L where
she can find a key of type t. She also knows a set of locations Π ⊆L where she can find a pizza.

ed82a955-33a6-4205-96f4-98a5556d11a7.name: Comparison Model Complexity Lower Bound
ed82a955-33a6-4205-96f4-98a5556d11a7.definition: A theoretical lower bound on the runtime of algorithms based on comparisons between elements, often used to prove that certain tasks cannot be done faster than a specific time complexity.

citations.snippet:
Problem 1.
Magikarp Jump
Maggie is running a Magikarp Jump contest. In each round, all n Magikarps jump once, and
each jump height is recorded. After each round, Maggie grabs a bag of berries, and allows the
highest-jumping Magikarps to choose one berry each, in decreasing order of jump height.
Help Maggie find an algorithm that, given an array of n jump heights and the number k of berries
in Maggie’s bag, outputs the order in which the highest-jumping Magikarps should choose their
berries.
(a) Prove that Maggie’s task must take Ω(n + k log n) time in the comparison model.
(b) Describe an asymptotically optimal algorithm for this task, and analyze its runtime.
(c) Implement your algorithm from part (b). Submit your code at https://alg.mit.edu.

52df26ba-0272-4698-b758-f75a24bd375d.definition: An s-t path such that the traveler is never within distance k of any mine located at certain intersections.

Problem 2.
Minesweeper
Inteleon is navigating a minefield with n intersections numbered from 0 through n −1 and m
two-way roads (with positive lengths) between the intersections, and his mission is to travel from
intersection s to t. He has received the intel that a set M of intersections each have a mine with a
proximity fuse. Say that an s-t path is k-safe if Inteleon can travel along it without ever being less
than distance k from any mine.
(a) Suppose Inteleon knows that the proximity fuses have range k, and he wants to com-
plete his mission as quickly as possible. Describe an O(n log n + m) algorithm to
find a shortest k-safe path, or output ⊥if no such path exists. Briefly (2-3 sentences)
justify correctness. You need not analyze runtime.

Problem 3.
A-Staryu
Staryu has a graph G = (V, E) with weight function w : E →[0, ∞) and wants to find a shortest
path from a vertex s to a vertex t. With limited psychic powers, Staryu has produced a heuristic
function h : V →[0, ∞), where h(v) is a guess for δ(v, t). Define the weight function w′(u, v) =
w(u, v) + h(v) −h(u), and let G′ be G reweighted with w′.
Staryu defines the algorithm A⋆(G, s, t, h) as follows: run Dijkstra on G′ (as defined above) from
s, but when t is removed from the priority queue, abort and return d(s, t) + h(s) −h(t).

Problem 2.
Munchlax has the Munchies
Munchlax has n containers of leftovers. Each container i of leftovers restores hi HP (non-negative)
when eaten. However, each container i also has an integer expiration time ti ≥1, after which it
cannot be eaten.
Assume that each container of leftovers takes 1 unit of time to eat, and that Munchlax can eat
continuously starting at time 0. In this problem we will find an algorithm to schedule Munchlax’s
meals (when and what to eat) to maximize HP restoration.

(b) Prove that any optimal schedule includes the container of leftovers with maximum hi.
(c) Give an O(n log n) greedy algorithm to find a schedule that maximizes HP restora-

76b993be-1e49-49ca-823d-0526141ad434.definition: The assumption that the algorithm works optimally for a smaller problem size, used to extend the proof to a larger problem size.

citations.snippet:
3. Inductive Step: Let’s prove that the greedy algorithm, GREEDY , is optimal for
n leftovers. First, let’s prove that we can schedule the leftovers at times ≤n −1.
Assume the optimal solution is S. If all the leftovers in S are scheduled to be eaten
at times ≤n −1, then we’re done. Otherwise, there’s at least one leftover, L that
expires at time t ≥n. With our induction hypothesis, we know that the remaining
leftovers can be scheduled at times ≤n−2, so we can schedule L at time n−1. As
a result, WLOG, all expiration times are ≤n. By GCP we can assume the optimal
solution S contains the greedy choice, and so does GREEDY . Therefore, we can
reduce the problem size and using induction, we can claim that the GREEDY
algorithm was not worse than the optimal S.

Merging Strings
(a) Given strings A, B and C, design a DP algorithm that checks in O(|A||B|) time
whether there is a way to merge A and B to produce C. You may assume that |C| =

For example, if A = abab, B = aabb and C = abaaabbb then the output should be
TRUE as C = aba+aabb+b where the first and last substrings come from A and the
middle one comes from B.

Problem 2.
Frieren
(a) Frieren has a row of treasure chests numbered 1 through n. There is an unknown s
such that chests 1 through s are safe, and the rest are mimics. Frieren can open chest i
and learn whether or not it is safe by spending a positive amount mi of mana.
Frieren must compute s without opening more than k mimics, given k and all of the
mi as inputs. Frieren will use the most efficient algorithm, in terms of the worst-case
total mana cost. For example, if k = 1, then the only correct algorithm is to open all
chests in increasing order of i, which costs

correctness beyond that.

sides by nb, we get nb ≤na.

6. Where does nlog n go in the asymptotic complexity table?
(a) Show that nlog n = Ω(na) for all constants a.
(b) Show that nlog n = O(2n).
Solution:
(a) For any constant a, we can choose n0 ≥1 such that log n ≥a for all n ≥n0. So, we
have nlog n ≥na for all n ≥n0.
(b) We can write nlog n as 2(log n)2. We see that n is asymptotically greater than (log n)2, so
nlog n = O(2n).

6. Use the substitution method to show that T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + n is O(n).
Solution: T(n) = Θ(n) by the substitution method. We want to prove T(n) ≤cn, so
assume it is true for values smaller than n. Substituting that in we have:
T(n) ≤cn/5 + 7cn/10 + n
T(n) ≤9cn/10 + n
We set this equal to cn = 9cn/10+n and solve for c = 10. Therefore T(n) ≤cn for c ≥10

• Let’s return to the divide-and-conquer algorithm for integer multiplication. We can solve the
recurrence relation T(n) ≤4T(n/2) + O(n) to obtain T(n) = O(n2). The algorithm also
uses Ω(n2) basic operations (count the addition operations at each recursive step).

that n was even, but then we made a recursive call to multiply n/2-digit integers, and n/2 may not
be even. This can be handled in (at least) two ways – padding with 0’s before starting the recursion,
and padding with 0’s at each step of the recursion.

3. In this class we will frequently prove correctness of algorithms via induction. Early in the
course, these proofs might seem unnecessary, because we will start by studying (relatively)
simple algorithms whose correctness is easy to see. However, it is important to get practice
with these inductive correctness proofs, because, as the course progresses, we will see more
and more sophisticated algorithms, whose correctness is far from obvious. We will convince
ourselves of their correctness via proofs.
With this in mind, prove by induction on n that Karatsuba’s algorithm run on two n-digit
integers x, y always returns x · y. The proof is relatively straightforward, but has a tricky
case which needs to be handled carefully.

Solution:
Proof. We use induction.
The base case is when there are no students in the room, in which case we return None.

algorithm is correct for size n −1. Now we split into 2 cases:

return this pair.

3. Provide a lower bound on the worst-case runtime for the birthday algorithm.
Solution:
As discussed in lecture, to prove a lower bound we need to find an example of
an input that makes the algorithm run for that amount of time, for each value of n. For this
problem, we want an input that achieves the worst case we thought of in the previous part:
run through every for loop and recursive call. This happens if all n students have different
birthdays, in which case the algorithm eventually returns None. In this case the algorithm
takes Θ(n2) time, so the worst-case runtime is Ω(n2).

citations.snippet:
2. Modify the Dynamic Array implementation of the SEQUENCE interface such that the opera-
tions insert first and delete first take O(1) amortized time alongside insert last
and delete last.
Solution:
We keep a single array with two pointers, start and end. Whenever we prepend, we move
the start pointer to the left if there is space. Similarly, we move the end pointer to the right
whenever we append. Deletions consist of moving the corresponding pointer in the opposite
direction and can be trivially implemented.
If there is no space for a given insert operation at a time when the array has n elements, we
allocate space such that there will be n free spaces to the left and n to the right of the array.
This ensures that we have enough space for at least n new insertions, which guarantees O(1)

1. Describe how to use a sorted array to implement the Set interface. What is the runtime of
each operation? (You can assume there is already plenty of space allocated for the array.)
Solution:
• build sorts the input array in O(n log n) time.
• find min and find max just return the first and last element in O(1) time.
• iter ord reads the array in order in O(n) time.
• find, find next, and find prev use binary search and so take O(log n) time.
• insert and delete are slow: they need to shift everything over, and take O(n) time.

aliases: Time Complexity of Find, Find Next, and Find Previous in Sorted Doubly Linked List

citations.snippet:
2. Describe how to use a sorted doubly linked list to implement the Set interface. What is the
runtime of each operation?
Solution:
• build sorts the input array in O(n log n) time.
• find min and find max take O(1) time because we have head and tail pointers.
• iter ord scans the list in order in O(n) time.
• find, find next, and find prev require scanning through the list, and so take
O(n) time.
• insert and delete also require scanning through the list to find the right spot, and
is O(n) time.

citations.snippet:
4. What is the brute force algorithm for solving this problem? What is its running time?
Solution: Use a nested loop: for each element in the array, count the number of elements
that have larger index in the array but smaller value. Sum up these counts to get the total
number of inversions. This algorithm is correct by exhaustive search. We can see that it
is Θ(n2) by analyzing the pseudo-code. Note that the algorithm takes the same time on all
inputs.

Solution: We will use Divide & Conquer in a way similar to Merge Sort. We divide the
array into two equal halves. The main observation is that an inversion is one of 2 types:

index comes from a different half. We count the intra-half inversions by invoking the algo-

3. Describe a linear time algorithm to sort a set n of strings, each having k English characters.
Solution: Use tuple sort to repeatedly sort the strings by each character from right to left with
counting sort, using the integers {0, . . . , 25} to represent the English alphabet. There are k
rounds of counting sort, and each round takes Θ(n + 26) = Θ(n) time, thus the algorithm
runs in Θ(nk) time. This running time is linear because the input size is Θ(nk).

745166dc-0d73-4530-afe7-8c2ef1e166ad.name: Radix Sort on Fixed-Length Strings
745166dc-0d73-4530-afe7-8c2ef1e166ad.definition: Sorting a list of fixed-length strings by iteratively sorting on each character position, often used for efficient linear-time sorting under constant-length assumptions.

citations.snippet:
0. For i = 0 to 7 inclusive, repeatedly perform Radix sort considering all characters of each
kerb except character i. Having the sorted kerbs (without considering character i), initialize
another variable s to be 1 that we’ll use to count the number of kerbs that are consecutive in
the sorted array and equal to each other, which makes them all similar to one another. We
then iterate through the kerbs and for every kerb, compare it to the next kerb. If the kerbs are
equal, we increase s by 1. Otherwise, we add s · (s −1)/2 to the variable count because we
have found s kerbs that are all similar to each other, and we reset the value of s to 1.
Since two kerbs are similar if they differ by exactly one character and no two kerbs are the
same, then they can differ only by a character at some i

5. Given an array of items A = (a0, . . . , an−1), describe an O(n log n)-time algorithm to con-
struct a binary search tree T containing the items in A such that T has height O(log n). You
may assume n is one less than a power of two.
Solution: Assume n = 2k −1. We begin by sorting the array A using merge sort. Then,
we build our binary tree as follows: If our current array has length 1, insert it into the tree.

next elements easily. By induction on k, the height of the resulting tree is k −1 ∈O(log n).

citations.snippet:
6. Let x and y be nodes in a BST, and suppose y is the successor of x and x has no right child.
Prove that y is an ancestor of x, and in particular x is in the left subtree of y.
Solution:
Let y be the successor of x and let z be the least common ancestor of x and y.
If z = y, then y is an ancestor of x. If z = x, since x has no right subtree, y must be in its
left subtree, so y ≤x which is impossible. Otherwise, x and y are in different subtrees of
z, which means z is between x and y, contradicting that y is the successor of x. The only
possible case is the first one, where y is the least common ancestor. Since x ≤y and y is an
ancestor of x, x must be in the left subtree of y.

in T, then moving through nodes and edges as we repeatedly find node.successor().

5. We saw how to create an iterator for an AVL tree in which the NEXT operation takes amor-
tized constant time but worst-case logarithmic time. Describe how to change the AVL tree
such that this NEXT operation takes worst-case constant time. The functionality of the AVL
tree (including asymptotic runtimes) should otherwise be unchanged.
Solution:
Each node should additionally carry a pointer to its predecessor and successor.
These can then be treated as doubly-linked list nodes as well as binary tree nodes. When we
delete a node from the binary tree, we can also have it delete itself from the linked list in the
usual way. For insertion, we observe that we can only ever add a leaf node, whose parent is
either its successor or predecessor. The parent node can then add into the linked list i

6fbcb760-9470-471d-8d4b-f8c9e821ac9c.name: Cross-Linking AVL Tree with Doubly-Linked List
6fbcb760-9470-471d-8d4b-f8c9e821ac9c.definition: A technique to augment AVL tree nodes with pointers to predecessor and successor to allow NEXT operation in iteration to run in worst-case constant time.
aliases: Cross-Linking AVL Tree with Doubly-Linked List
Cross-linking AVL tree with linked list

citations.snippet:
5. We saw how to create an iterator for an AVL tree in which the NEXT operation takes amor-
tized constant time but worst-case logarithmic time. Describe how to change the AVL tree
such that this NEXT operation takes worst-case constant time. The functionality of the AVL
tree (including asymptotic runtimes) should otherwise be unchanged.
Solution:
Each node should additionally carry a pointer to its predecessor and successor.
These can then be treated as doubly-linked list nodes as well as binary tree nodes. When we
delete a node from the binary tree, we can also have it delete itself from the linked list in the
usual way. For insertion, we observe that we can only ever add a leaf node, whose parent is
either its successor or predecessor. The parent node can then add into the linked list i

f3858499-f5a6-4276-9a10-722490bdcc0f.definition: A combined data structure linking an AVL tree keyed by k1 and a hash table keyed by k2 to allow efficient INSERT, FIND, and DELETE operations by either key.
aliases: Cross-Linked Data Structure for Dual-Key Access
AVL Tree and Hash Table Combination

citations.snippet:
6. Suppose you have some items x, each of which has one comparable key k1(x) and one
hashable key k2(x). Assume that both keys are unique. Describe an unordered SET data
structure that can INSERT efficiently and can FIND or DELETE efficiently using either key.
What is the runtime of each operation, and is it worst-case, amortized, and/or expected?
Solution: This time, we cross-link an AVL tree (keyed by k1) with a hash table (keyed by
k2). Each chain in the hash table will be an linked list (as in the previous exercise) of tree
nodes. FIND by k1 uses one AVL FIND so takes worst-case O(log n) time. FIND by k2 uses
one hash FIND so takes expected O(1) time. INSERT and DELETE use dynamic operations
on both data structures so take amortized and expected O(log n) time.

citations.snippet:
1. Suppose you want a data structure that maintains a SET of integers, with the additional
operation CLOSEST(), which should in constant time return the minimum positive difference
between two elements of your SET.
(a) Clearly CLOSEST() cannot be computed from scratch in constant time. A natural strat-
egy to attempt in such a situation is to make it an augmentation. Explain why CLOS-
EST() cannot be an augmentation.
Solution: An augmentation must be computable from data and augmentation values at
nodes up to a constant depth, say d. A complete binary tree containing the even integers
between −2d+1 and 2d+1 exclusive is then indistinguishable from one containing those
same elements except with 2 replaced by 1. However, CLOSEST() should output 2 in
the former case and 1 in the latter.

Solution:

number of 1 bits in its subtree. We can compute this in O(1) time from the augmentations
stored at its children: add its childrens’ subtree ones, and add one if A has a 1.

citations.snippet:
5. Given an unweighted graph G = (V, E) in which some edges are red and some are blue, find
a path from s to t with the minimal number of red edges.
Solution: We combine BFS and DFS. The main idea is that using a DEQUE, we can BFS
w.r.t. red edges while simultaneously condensing blue edges using DFS.
• Initialize a DEQUE Q = [s], d(s) = 0, and P(s) = ⊥
• While Q is non-empty:
– Remove the first element u from Q
– For each unvisited out-neighbor v of u:
* set P(v) = u
* if (u, v) is red, set d(v) = d(u) + 1 and append v to Q
* if (u, v) is blue, instead set d(v) = d(u) and prepend v to Q
• Follow parent pointers from t and output the resulting path
Correctness and runtime proofs are as DFS and BFS.

citations.snippet:
2. Given a directed graph G, construct and analyze the runtime of an algorithm to create graph
GR which is identical to G but with all the edges reversed. Solve for both an adjacency list
and adjacency matrix representation.
Solution: First we describe how to construct the adjacency representation of GR given that
of G. We loop through each vertex v in G. For each neighbor u of v, we add v to the list of
neighbors of u in GR. This takes O(|V | + |E|) time.
For adjacency matrices, the adjacency matrix for GR is simply the transpose of the adjacency
matrix for G. It takes O(|V |2) time to construct the transpose because you need to go through
all O(|V |2) entries in the matrix.
Both runtimes are linear.

f273ad73-77ea-4de4-8675-56931801f24f.name: Depth-First Search (DFS) Implementation Using a Stack
f273ad73-77ea-4de4-8675-56931801f24f.definition: A method to perform DFS traversal by using a stack data structure to manage vertices, utilizing push and pop operations to explore graph vertices.
aliases: Depth-First Search (DFS) Implementation Using a Stack

citations.snippet:
4. Describe how to implement DFS using a STACK as the main data structure. Remember that
a STACK supports the push and pop operations.
Solution:
Initialize the Stack to contain just the source vertex. Repeat while the stack is
nonempty:
• pop the first element off the stack.
– If it is marked, move to the next round
– If it is not marked, mark it as visited. Besides, for each of its neighbors, push the
neighbor to the stack.
.
The time complexity of this implementation is also O(|E|) because we process each vertex
and each edge at most once, and (for single-source) discover at most |E| + 1 vertices. We
could do the same for a full (rather than single-source) DFS, which would still take time
O(|V | + |E|).

citations.snippet:
1. Design an algorithm to build the condensation graph GC = (VC, EC) of G = (V, E).
Solution:
First find the connected components of the graph, as described in lecture. For
each connected component, designate one of its nodes to be its leader. We will use the
leaders to represent connected components, so VC is the set of leaders. Let the leader of
some node u be L(u).
Now iterate over all edges u →v in E, and add the edge L(u) →L(v) to EC if L(u)̸ = L(v).
This takes O(|V | + |E|) time.

exactly one box. There’s at least one copy of each box’s key, but for some boxes there may

contain multiple keys. Boxes can also be forced open with a rusty crowbar. Design an

the other boxes.

citations.snippet:
1. Totodile has k PP to spend and wants to go to Tangelo Island. Design an O(k|E|) time
algorithm to decide whether Totodile can reach Tangelo Island.
Solution:
This reduces to SPSP by using a variant of graph duplication that subdivides
edges instead of duplicating the original vertices. We assume WLOG that G is connected;
o/w we can prune unreachable vertices in O(|E|) time using e.g. DFS.
• Construct a graph G1 by subdividing every edge {u, v} into a cu,v-edge chain of edges
if cu,v ≤k (instead remove the edge if cu,v > k).
• BFS in G1 from Shamouti Island to compute the distance d to Tangelo Island.
• Output d ≤k.
G1 has at most k|E| edges and at most |V | + |E|(k −1) vertices, so constructing it takes
Θ(k|E|) time. BFS also takes Θ(k|E|) time. If d ≤k, then Totodile can reach Tangelo

2. In a graph G = (V, E) with positive edge weights, there are special nodes, s1, s2, . . . , sk,
where k is not necessarily a constant. For every node v in the graph, we want to find the
distance from the closest special node to v. Describe a O(|E| + |V | log |V |) algorithm to do
so.
Solution: We add a so-called “supernode” s∗as another vertex to G. We connect s∗to each
of s1, s2, . . . , sk with an edge of weight 0. This effectively forces the shortest path (or any
other path for that matter) from s∗to v to start at a special node. In addition, setting the edge
weights to 0 means that the shortest distance from s∗to v will be equal to the shortest of the
distances from s1, s2, . . . , sk to v. Hence, we can just run Dijkstra from s∗and output the
shortest path distances between s∗and v

citations.snippet:
2. In a graph G = (V, E) with positive edge weights, there are special nodes, s1, s2, . . . , sk,
where k is not necessarily a constant. For every node v in the graph, we want to find the
distance from the closest special node to v. Describe a O(|E| + |V | log |V |) algorithm to do
so.
Solution: We add a so-called “supernode” s∗as another vertex to G. We connect s∗to each
of s1, s2, . . . , sk with an edge of weight 0. This effectively forces the shortest path (or any
other path for that matter) from s∗to v to start at a special node. In addition, setting the edge
weights to 0 means that the shortest distance from s∗to v will be equal to the shortest of the
distances from s1, s2, . . . , sk to v. Hence, we can just run Dijkstra from s∗and output the
shortest path distances between s∗and v

3e4b0f5d-2107-4aff-afda-9d7f688fc8e6.name: Safest path problem with probabilistic edge failure
3e4b0f5d-2107-4aff-afda-9d7f688fc8e6.definition: Finding a path in a graph that minimizes the probability of an undesired event occurring on any edge along the path, assuming independent edge probabilities.

4. Ash is trying to cycle from Pallet Town to Viridian City without destroying Misty’s bike.
For every trail e in the area, he knows the probability p(e) of destroying the bike if he cycles
along e. Help Ash find the safest path to Viridian City (the path that minimizes his probabil-
ity of destroying the bike). Assume that all probabilities are independent and that arithmetic
operations take constant time.
Solution: Construct a graph having a vertex v for every trail intersection, and weight each
edge (trail) e with w(e) = 1−p(e). Run Dijkstra using (0, 1), max, ×, 1, 0 instead of [0, ∞],
min, +, 0, ∞, respectively. If n is the number of intersections and m the number of trails in
the graph, then Dijkstra will take O(m + n log n) time using a Fibonacci Heap.

Let G = (V, E) be a directed weighted graph with no negative cycles. We say a vertex v is
useful if there are two vertices s, t̸ = v such that v is on a minimum-weight path from s to t.

(If there are multiple minimum-weight paths from s to t, v only has to be on one of them.)

begin by running Johnson’s algorithm. This takes time O(|V ||E|+|V |2 log |V |) = O(|V |3).

vertex would be too slow.)

to choose from, and she knows which pairs of these people know each other. She wants to
invite as many people as possible subject to the constraint:
For each guest, there should be at least five other guests that they already know.
Describe and analyze an O(n2)-time algorithm that computes the largest possible number of
guests Alice can invite, given a list of pairs, where a pair (i, j) represents guest number i and
guest number j knowing each other.
Solution: Observation: If there’s a guest who knows < 5 people, they cannot come to the
party.
Greedy Choice: Remove any guest who does not currently meet the constraint.
GCP: Any guest that does not meet the constraint is not in any optimal solution.

518b0420-89ab-45fe-b143-70793d87644a.definition: Given an arithmetic expression without parentheses with operators + and ×, find how to parenthesize it to maximize the final value.

citations.snippet:
Recitation 20

Exercise 2: Arithmetic Parenthesization
You are given an arithmetic expression without any parentheses: a0 ∗1 a1 ∗2 a2 · · · ∗n−1 an−1,
where each ai is an integer and each operator ∗i ∈{+, ×}. Describe a dynamic program to place
parentheses (with correct syntax) to maximize the value of the resulting expression. For example:
8 + 4 × 3 + 5
→
(8 + 4) × (3 + 5)
=
96
8 + (−4) × 3 + (−5)
→
8 +
�(−4) × (3 + (−5))

=
16
Solution: After placing parentheses, the ‘components’ of the expression are subarray of the form
ai ∗i+1 ai+1 · · · ∗j−1 aj−1. We will have subproblems indexed by i and j for the maximum value of
this subarray.
But this isn’t enough! For example, (−3) × (−3) = 9 > (−2) × (−2) = 4, so we might want to
minimize or maximize a subarray, depending on other subarrays.

ai ∗i+1 ai+1 · · · ∗j−1 aj−1. We will have subproblems indexed by i and j for the maximum value of

minimize or maximize a subarray, depending on other subarrays.

53d0c0cd-33cc-4a85-b112-6a7e30dbaf98.definition: Method to count the number of minimum-weight paths from a source s to vertex v using exactly k edges, based on subproblems defining minimum weights and path counts for fixed edge counts.

citations.snippet:
from Lecture 20 to count the minimum-weight paths that use
exactly k edges for each possible value of k. We need to say exactly k instead of at most k to avoid
counting paths that use fewer edges multiple times.
Subproblems: For 0 ≤k < n and v ∈V ,
• let δk(v) be the minimum weight of a path from s to v that uses exactly k edges, and
• let x(v, k) be the number of paths from s to v that use exactly k edges and have weight
δk(v) (i.e. the number of minimum-weight k-edge paths).
Relate: Let k ≥1. We consider each possible last edge on a k-edge path from s to v. This gives
δk(v) = min{δk−1(u) + w(u, v) | (u, v) ∈E}.
To count the minimum-weight paths, observe each minimum-weight k −1-edge path to u
becomes a minimum-weight k-edge path to v when we add (u, v), provided that δk−1(u) +

2. Adapt the Subset Sum algorithm to work on sets containing negative numbers.

We will describe a DP very similar to the one for Subset Sum in lecture. The

4. Close Partition. (optional) Given a set of n positive integers A, describe an algorithm to
partition A into two subsets A1 and A2 such that the absolute difference
   P A1 −P A2
  
between their sums is minimized.
Solution:
As before, let S be the sum of all the numbers. Assume by symmetry that
P A1 ≤P A2, so P A1 ≤S/2. Then the problem is equivalent to finding a subset A1 with
the maximum possible sum that’s no more than S/2.
As before, run the Subset Sum dynamic program using T = S/2. Fer each t ≤S/2, this
tells us whether there is a subset with sum t. We find the largest t for which there is such a
subset, and then reconstruct the subset using our parent pointers.
The runtime is dominated by the dynamic program, so it’s still O(nS).

f13f1967-4525-415a-b702-9b5423fd7447.definition: An algorithm that solves the Partition problem by computing the total sum S and then solving the Subset Sum problem with target S/2 to find a subset that sums to half the total.

citations.snippet:
1. Describe an algorithm to solve Partition: Given a set of n positive integers A, determine
whether A can be partitioned into two subsets A1 and A2 of equal sum.
For example, A = {1, 3, 4, 12, 19, 21, 22} can be partitioned into A1 = {1, 19, 21} and
A2 = {3, 4, 12, 22}, which both have sum 41.
Solution: Let S be the sum of all the number in A. In any partition, P A1 + P A2 = S.
That means P A1 = P A2 if and only if P A1 = S/2. So the problem is equivalent to
looking for a subset of A with sum S/2, so we can solve it by running the algorithm for
Subset Sum on A with T = S/2.

9f5b0959-5f3f-4429-8ae8-a82ade32f69b.name: NP Class Verification
9f5b0959-5f3f-4429-8ae8-a82ade32f69b.definition: The method by which a certificate can be checked quickly (in polynomial time) to verify membership in NP problems.

citations.snippet:
1. In an undirected graph, a clique is a set of vertices such that every pair of them is connected
by an edge. Given an undirected graph G = (V, E) and an integer k, CLIQUE asks whether
G has a clique of size k.
Show that CLIQUE is in NP by designing a verifier for it: specify what the certificates
represent, describe the verifier itself, analyze its runtime, and argue that the verifier takes
polynomial time in n, the size of the input.
Solution: A certificate is a set of nodes U which is a clique of size k.
The verifier first checks that |U| = k. Then it checks that for all u, v ∈U, there is an edge
(u, v) ∈E.
This takes O(k2) time. Since k ≤|V | ≤n (because the input includes G which has size
|V | + |E|), this is O(n2).
It turns out that CLIQUE is NP-complete!

1cfa0041-c93e-4560-8ba8-5e405c52d25d.definition: A technique to prove undecidability by showing that if a problem was decidable, then the HALT problem would be decidable too, which is a contradiction.

Exercise: Acceptance Problem
The following problem, similar to the Halting Problem, is called the Acceptance Problem.
ACCEPT
Input: a binary string, interpreted as a pair (A, x)
– A is an algorithm
– x is some other binary string
Output:
– YES if A(x) eventually halts and outputs YES
– NO otherwise, i.e. if A(x) outputs NO or doesn’t halt
(a) Prove that ACCEPT is recognizable. That is, prove that there exists an algorithm B
such that B(A, x) = YES iff ACCEPT(A, x) = YES.
(b) Prove that ACCEPT is undecidable by reducing from HALT.

scribed in the greedy choice.
Proof. Consider an optimal solution S. By Lemma 2 we know S uses x in some path p, and
by Lemma 1 we know that no other path in S goes through any descendant of x.
We construct a new solution S′ by replacing p with the path that starts at the deepest de-
scendant of x. As in Lemma 2, this path stays in the subtree under x, and ends at x. In
particular, it doesn’t intersect any other paths in S. So S′ is a valid solution, S′ makes the
greedy choice, and S′ uses as many paths as S so is also optimal.

Exercise: Acceptance Problem
The following problem, similar to the Halting Problem, is called the Acceptance Problem.
ACCEPT
Input: a binary string, interpreted as a pair (A, x)
– A is an algorithm
– x is some other binary string
Output:
– YES if A(x) eventually halts and outputs YES
– NO otherwise, i.e. if A(x) outputs NO or doesn’t halt
(a) Prove that ACCEPT is recognizable. That is, prove that there exists an algorithm B
such that B(A, x) = YES iff ACCEPT(A, x) = YES.
Solution: B(A, x) runs A(x) and outputs the result (if any). Then B(A, x) = YES
iff A(x) = YES iff ACCEPT(A, x) = YES as desired.

8e1d409c-4d32-4508-9679-48dc29ea6ab9.name: Damage of a House in Porkland
8e1d409c-4d32-4508-9679-48dc29ea6ab9.definition: For a given house with b bricks, the number of houses that would fall if the wolf blows on it in an easterly direction, considering the bricks count of the houses to the east.
aliases: Damage of a House in Porkland

citations.snippet:
Problem 1.
Brick Blowing
Porkland is a community of pigs who live in n houses lined up along one side of a long, straight
street running east to west. Every house in Porkland was built from straw and bricks, but some
houses were built with more bricks than others. One day, a wolf arrives in Porkland and all the
pigs run inside their homes to hide. Unfortunately for the pigs, this wolf is extremely skilled at
blowing down pig houses, aided by a strong wind already blowing from west to east. If the wolf
blows in an easterly direction on a house containing b bricks, that house will fall down, along with
every house east of it containing strictly fewer than b bricks. For every house in Porkland, the wolf
wants to know its damage, i.e., the number of houses that would fall were he to blow on it

4dc15ad1-f15a-406b-80ff-43333488ff55.name: Frog Jump Problem
4dc15ad1-f15a-406b-80ff-43333488ff55.definition: A problem where a frog must jump on stones placed in increasing positions along a river to reach the last stone, with constraints on jump lengths based on the previous jump.

citations.snippet:
Problem 1.
A frog is attempting to cross a river by jumping on stones. The river is divided into units of length,
and at each unit, there may or may not be a stone. The frog can jump on a stone, but not on water.
The frog begins on the first stone and must reach the last stone. If the frog’s last jump had length
k, then the next jump must be of length k −1, k, or k + 1 units (but all jumps must be positive).
The frog may only move in the forward direction and begins by making a jump of length 1 unit.
Given an array stones of integers in strictly increasing order, representing the positions of the
stones in the river, determine whether the frog can reach the final stone.
Example 1. Input: stones = [0,1,3,5,6,8,11,15]
Output: true
Explanation: The frog can jump from position 0 →1 →3 →5 →6 →8

c08dc6f1-218d-47c7-aae5-7f87aba2037b.definition: The number of houses that would fall when blowing on a given house, considering the rules of the Brick Blowing problem where houses east of the blown house fall if they have fewer bricks.
aliases: House Damage in Brick Blowing Problem

citations.snippet:
Problem 1.
Brick Blowing
Porkland is a community of pigs who live in n houses lined up along one side of a long, straight
street running east to west. Every house in Porkland was built from straw and bricks, but some
houses were built with more bricks than others. One day, a wolf arrives in Porkland and all the
pigs run inside their homes to hide. Unfortunately for the pigs, this wolf is extremely skilled at
blowing down pig houses, aided by a strong wind already blowing from west to east. If the wolf
blows in an easterly direction on a house containing b bricks, that house will fall down, along with
every house east of it containing strictly fewer than b bricks. For every house in Porkland, the wolf
wants to know its damage, i.e., the number of houses that would fall were he to blow on it

Given three arrays A, B, C, each containing n integers, give an O(n2)-time algorithm to find
whether some a ∈A, some b ∈B, and some c ∈C have zero sum, i.e., a + b + c = 0. State
whether your running time is worst-case, expected, and/or amortized.

Problem 2.
[15 points] Triple Sum
Given three arrays A, B, C, each containing n integers, give an O(n2)-time algorithm to find
whether some a ∈A, some b ∈B, and some c ∈C have zero sum, i.e., a + b + c = 0. State
whether your running time is worst-case, expected, and/or amortized.
Solution: We present both expected and worst-case solutions (both were accepted for full points).
Expected Time
For each pair of numbers (a, b) ∈A × B, store a + b in a hash table H. Then return Yes if −c
appears in H for any c ∈C, and return No otherwise.
Correctness: If any −c appears in H for any c ∈C, then −c = a′ + b′ for some (a′, b′) ∈A × B
so a′ + b′ + c = 0. Otherwise, there is no c ∈C for which −c = a′ + b′ for any (a′, b′) ∈A × B.
Running Time: There are O(n2) pairs in A × B, so inserting them into H t

labeled path is its path weight plus wc (a positive integer) each time the path changes color.

an efficient algorithm to compute a minimum color cost path from s to t.

978ab880-394a-4c28-abb3-f12790f665f5.definition: A graph model representing planets as nodes and three types of tunnels (space, space-time, and time tunnels) as directed edges with associated costs and time transitions.
aliases: Directed Graph with Time and Space Tunnels

Problem 3.
A Tour on the 4-dimensional Galaxy0
The 4-dimensional galaxy allows its visitors to travel from planet to planet (via directed space-
tunnels). What is cool about the 4-dimensional galaxy is that there are also tunnels that allow
travelers to travel into the future. There are space-time-tunnels which allow travelers to travel
from one planet to another planet and arriving one year into the future. Finally, there are also
time-tunnels that allow travelers to travel several years into the future (but stay in the same planet).
Each tunnel t has a cost ct (which can be either positive or negative). Each space-tunnel t is defined
by a pair of planets (pt, qt). Each time-space-tunnel t is also specified by a pair of planets (pt, qt).
Finally, each time-tunnel t is specified by a plane

Let G = (V, E) be a directed graph, not necessarily weakly-connected. For a vertex v ∈V , define
ρ(v) to be the number of nodes reachable from v (including v). Describe an efficient algorithm

You have N ropes of different lengths. Any two ropes of length x and y can be

algorithm to connect all N ropes into one rope with minimum cost. You do not need to prove

Problem 3.
A frog is attempting to cross a river by jumping on stones. The river is divided into units of length,
and at each unit, there may or may not be a stone. The frog can jump on a stone, but not on water.
The frog begins on the first stone and must reach the last stone. If the frog’s last jump had length
k, then the next jump must be of length k −1, k, or k + 1 units (but all jumps must be positive).
The frog may only move in the forward direction and begins by making a jump of length 1 unit.
Given an array stones of integers in strictly increasing order, representing the positions of the
stones in the river, determine whether the frog can reach the final stone.

Output: true
Explanation: The frog can jump from position 0 →1 →3 →5 →6 →8

def count_paths(L):
    '''
    Input:  L | size-n direct access array of size-n direct access arrays
              | each L[i][j] is either 'V', '+', or ' '
              | for virus, upgrade, or empty respectively
    Output: p | the number of distinct optimal paths in L
              | starting from (0,0) and ending at (n-1,n-1)
    '''
    p = 0

    # Solution

    n = len(L)
    NEG_INF = -10**9

    dp = [[(NEG_INF, 0) for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(n)]

    if L[0][0] == 'V':
        return 0

    start_up = 1 if L[0][0] == '+' else 0
    dp[0][0] = (start_up, 1)

    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            if L[i][j] == 'V':
                continue
            if i == 0 and j == 0:
                continue

            add = 1 if L[i][j] == '+' else 0

def magikarp_jump(heights, k):
    """Find the largest k elements of heights
    Input:

        k :: int
            Length of output sequence in range [0, len(heights))
    Output:
        highest :: [int]
            Length k array of largest elements of heights in decreasing order

    # Edge case: no prizes
    if k <= 0:
        return []
    if k >= len(heights):
        return sorted(heights, reverse=True)

def quarter_partition(A):
    '''
    Input:  A :: [int]
            List of positive integers
    Output: q :: int
            maximum quality of a 4-partition of A
    '''
    n = len(A)

    if n == 0:
        return 0

    from collections import defaultdict

    dp = [set() for _ in range(n + 1)]
    dp[0].add((0, 0, 0, 0))

    for i in range(n):
        for state in dp[i]:
            for j in range(4):
                new_state = list(state)
                new_state[j] += A[i]
                new_state = tuple(sorted(new_state))
                dp[i + 1].add(new_state)

    max_quality = 0
    for state in dp[n]:
        min_sum = min(state)
        max_quality = max(max_quality, min_sum)

    return max_quality
